knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Write the underlying partial-field elements as \(G\cup\{0\}\). A matrix \(A\) over \(R\) is a \(\mathbb P\)-matrix when the determinant of every square submatrix belongs to \(G\cup\{0\}\). A \(\mathbb P\)-representation of \(M\), relative to \(B\), is a matrix \([I_B\mid A]\) with \(A\) a \(\mathbb P\)-matrix such that, for every \(r(M)\)-element subset \(X\) of the column set, \(X\) is a basis of \(M\) if and only if the corresponding maximal determinant is nonzero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partial-field representation is a normalized matrix whose square determinants are partial-field elements and whose nonzero maximal minors are exactly the matroid bases.
knowledge_statements.title: Partial-Field Representations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits, but the determinant and normalized-representation conventions are specialized and require an authoritative source with a precise locator.

children.title: Characteristic Sets
children.top_down_role: Sets of field characteristics supporting representation of a matroid.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Char}(M)\subseteq\{0\}\cup\{p:p\text{ is prime}\}\) records exactly the characteristics admitting a field representation of \(M\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characteristics of fields, without restricting field size or extension degree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The characteristic set of \(M\) is \[\operatorname{Char}(M)=\{c\in\{0\}\cup\{p:p\text{ is prime}\}:\text{ there exists a field }K\text{ with }\operatorname{char}(K)=c\text{ over which }M\text{ is representable}\}.\] Membership records existence over at least one field of the stated characteristic; it does not assert representability over every field of that characteristic. In particular, field-size restrictions within a fixed characteristic are not captured by \(\operatorname{Char}(M)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The characteristic set lists exactly those field characteristics for which at least one field representation of the matroid exists.
knowledge_statements.title: Characteristic Sets

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly distinguishes existence over some field from representability over every field of a characteristic, but it has no cited source.

children.title: Representation Rigidity
children.top_down_role: Constraints on variation among inequivalent representations.

assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a finite rank-\(r\) matroid on a labeled ground set \(E\).
\(K\) is a field over which \(M\) is representable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\) is projectively rigid over \(K\) exactly when all its labeled \(K\)-representations lie in one projective-equivalence class.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projective rigidity for labeled representations over one fixed field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Two full-rank \(K\)-matrices \(A\) and \(A'\), with columns labeled by \(E\), are projectively equivalent when \(A'=UAD\) for some \(U\in\operatorname{GL}_r(K)\) and some invertible diagonal \(E\times E\) matrix \(D\). The matroid \(M\) is projectively rigid over \(K\) when every pair of labeled \(K\)-representations of \(M\) is projectively equivalent. This convention permits elementary row changes and independent nonzero column scalings, but does not identify representations using a nontrivial automorphism of \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matroid is projectively rigid over a field when every labeled representation differs only by invertible row operations and nonzero column scalings.
knowledge_statements.title: Representation Rigidity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is internally precise for labeled representations, but rigidity conventions can differ regarding field automorphisms and relabeling; the selected convention requires a source.

children.title: Partial-Field Universality
children.top_down_role: Coordination of field-specific representations through universal partial-field data.

assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a finite matroid admitting a partial-field representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Universality means that every partial-field representation of \(M\), up to the stated equivalence, is induced from \(A_M\) by a homomorphism out of \(\mathbb U_M\).

notation.meaning: A universal partial field for M

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Universal mapping property for partial-field representations of a fixed matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A partial field \(\mathbb U_M\), equipped with a \(\mathbb U_M\)-representation \(A_M\) of \(M\), is universal for \(M\) when the following property holds: for every partial field \(\mathbb P\) and every \(\mathbb P\)-representation \(A\) of \(M\), there exists a partial-field homomorphism \(\varphi:\mathbb U_M\to\mathbb P\) such that the entrywise image \(\varphi(A_M)\) is equivalent to \(A\) under basis changes, row operations, and nonzero column scalings allowed for partial-field representations. The pair \((\mathbb U_M,A_M)\) is unique only up to the corresponding universal isomorphism.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A universal partial field parametrizes every partial-field representation of a fixed matroid through homomorphisms and standard representation equivalences.
knowledge_statements.title: Partial-Field Universality

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The asserted universal property, existence scope, representation equivalence, and uniqueness formulation are specialized and cannot be validated without an authoritative citation.

children.title: Characteristic-Set Realizability
children.top_down_role: Structural boundaries on characteristic sets arising from matroid representations.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) is characteristic-set realizable if and only if \(S=\operatorname{Char}(M)\) for some finite matroid \(M\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existential realizability by finite matroids; no classification of realizable sets is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \(S\) is characteristic-set realizable when there exists a finite matroid \(M\) such that \[S=\operatorname{Char}(M)=\{\operatorname{char}(K):K\text{ is a field over which }M\text{ is representable}\}.\] Thus realizability requires both directions: every \(c\in S\) occurs as the characteristic of at least one representing field, and no field whose characteristic lies outside \(S\) represents \(M\). The quantifier ranges over all fields, not merely finite fields or prime fields.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set of characteristics is realizable when it is exactly the set of characteristics of fields representing some finite matroid.
knowledge_statements.title: Characteristic-Set Realizability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement gives a coherent existential definition, but no source establishes the terminology. Its mathematical role is a definition rather than a condition, so the selected content kind also requires correction after sourcing.

children.title: Graphic-Matroid Recognition
children.top_down_role: Recognition criteria, input regimes, certificates, plus obstruction boundaries for graphic matroids.

knowledge_statements.title: Graphic-Matroid Recognition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision problem for a finite labeled matroid supplied by an independence oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite matroid presented by an independence oracle. The graphic-matroid recognition problem asks whether there exists a finite undirected multigraph \(G\), with a bijection \(\phi:E\to E(G)\), such that \(X\in\mathcal I\) exactly when \(\phi(X)\) is a forest of \(G\). A positive output may additionally return such a graph \(G\) and bijection \(\phi\); loops of \(M\) correspond to graph loops, and parallel matroid elements correspond to parallel graph edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Decide whether the input matroid is the cycle matroid of a graph and, in the constructive version, return such a graph.
assumptions_latex: Access to \(M\) is through an independence oracle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is graphic}\iff \exists G,\phi\;\forall X\subseteq E:\ X\in\mathcal I\iff \phi(X)\text{ is a forest of }G.\)

notation.meaning: cycle matroid of the graph G
bijection from matroid elements to graph edges

review_flags: Exact recognition theorem and oracle-complexity source are not supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The decision-problem definition is mathematically coherent and fits the recognition leaf, but no inspectable source supports the oracle model or constructive-output formulation.

children.title: Cographic-Matroid Recognition
children.top_down_role: Recognition through dual structure, representation access, plus certifying outcomes.

knowledge_statements.title: Cographic-Matroid Recognition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recognition through duality with the cycle matroid of a graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite matroid presented by an independence oracle. The cographic-matroid recognition problem asks whether there exist a finite undirected multigraph \(G\) and a bijection \(\phi:E\to E(G)\) such that \(M\cong M(G)^*\). Equivalently, it asks whether the dual matroid \(M^*\) is graphic. In the constructive version, a positive output returns \(G\) and \(\phi\), thereby representing the cocircuits of \(M\) as the cycles of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Decide whether the input matroid is the dual of a graph's cycle matroid; construct the graph when requested.
assumptions_latex: Access to \(M\) is through an independence oracle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is cographic}\iff M^*\text{ is graphic}\iff \exists G:\ M\cong M(G)^*.\)
review_flags: Exact constructive recognition source and oracle model require confirmation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dual characterization is correct and the definition fits the recognition leaf, but the oracle and constructive formulations have no cited source.

children.title: Regular-Matroid Recognition
children.top_down_role: Recognition regimes based on regular representations, excluded minors, or structural decomposition.

knowledge_statements.title: Regular-Matroid Recognition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision problem using representability over every field as the regularity criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite matroid given by an independence oracle. Regular-matroid recognition asks whether \(M\) is representable over every field. Equivalently, it asks whether \(M\) has a real matrix representation that is projectively equivalent to a totally unimodular matrix. A constructive positive output consists of a totally unimodular matrix \(A\), whose columns are labeled by \(E\), such that \(X\subseteq E\) is independent in \(M\) exactly when the columns \(A_X\) are linearly independent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Decide whether a matroid is representable over every field and, constructively, return a totally unimodular matrix representation.
assumptions_latex: Access to \(M\) is through an independence oracle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is regular}\iff M\text{ is representable over every field}.\)

notation.meaning: submatrix formed by columns labeled by X

review_flags: A source for the equivalence and the precise recognition algorithm is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The regularity criterion and constructive matrix formulation require an authoritative source, particularly for the oracle-input reconstruction claim and the projective-equivalence wording.

children.title: Recognition-Class Relationships
children.top_down_role: Containments, dual correspondences, plus boundaries separating the three recognition tasks.

knowledge_statements.title: Recognition-Class Relationships
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Containment and duality relations among graphic, cographic, and regular matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every finite matroid \(M\), graphicness and cographicness are exchanged by duality, while regularity is preserved by duality. Every graphic matroid and every cographic matroid is regular. Consequently,
\[
M\text{ graphic}\iff M^*\text{ cographic},\qquad M\text{ regular}\iff M^*\text{ regular},
\]
and
\[
\{\text{graphic matroids}\}\cup\{\text{cographic matroids}\}\subseteq\{\text{regular matroids}\}.
\]
Neither inclusion of the graphic or cographic class in the regular class is an equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Graphic and cographic classes are dual; both lie properly inside the dual-closed class of regular matroids.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ graphic}\iff M^*\text{ cographic}\), and graphic or cographic \(M\) implies regular \(M\).

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

review_flags: Properness examples should be checked against the cited chapter.

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

knowledge_statements.title: Field-Representability Decision Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representability over a fixed field for an oracle-presented finite matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a field \(\mathbb F\). Given a finite matroid \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\), the \(\mathbb F\)-representability decision problem asks whether there exist an integer \(r\) and a matrix \(A\in\mathbb F^{r\times E}\), with columns labeled by \(E\), such that for every \(X\subseteq E\),
\[
X\in\mathcal I\iff \operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb F}(A_X)=|X|.
\]
The constructive version must return such a matrix when the answer is positive; its computational complexity depends essentially on how \(M\) and \(\mathbb F\) are encoded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed field, decide whether the matroid's independent sets are exactly the linearly independent column sets of some matrix.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb F\) and its effective encoding are fixed or supplied explicitly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is }\mathbb F\text{-representable}\iff \exists A\in\mathbb F^{r\times E}\;\forall X\subseteq E:\ X\in\mathcal I\iff \operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb F}(A_X)=|X|.\)

notation.meaning: columns of A indexed by X

review_flags: Complexity varies with the field and input model; no precise source locator was supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fixed-field representability decision problem is precisely stated and definition is an appropriate content kind, but no source supports the formulation or its encoding qualification.

children.title: Representation Reconstruction
children.top_down_role: Recovery of a representation from oracle data, structural data, or partial representation data.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation Reconstruction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-to-matrix reconstruction over a specified field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a finite matroid \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) through an independence oracle and a field \(\mathbb F\), under the promise that \(M\) is \(\mathbb F\)-representable. A representation-reconstruction algorithm queries the oracle and either outputs a matrix \(A\in\mathbb F^{r(M)\times E}\) satisfying
\[
X\in\mathcal I\iff \operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb F}(A_X)=|X|\quad\text{for every }X\subseteq E,
\]
or reports that reconstruction is unsupported under its stated field or access model. Correctness requires every returned matrix to represent the labeled input matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given oracle access and a representability promise, construct a labeled matrix whose column dependencies reproduce the matroid.
assumptions_latex: An independence oracle for \(M\) is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\text{ output}\implies M(A)=M.\)
review_flags: Existence and complexity of reconstruction depend on the field and oracle model.
A concrete reconstruction algorithm source is needed.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record gives an output specification rather than a concrete reconstruction algorithm. Whether reconstruction is possible from an independence oracle depends materially on the field and access model, so a precise sourced algorithm is required.

children.title: Representation Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Comparison regimes for deciding whether representations encode the same matroid structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projective equivalence for labeled matrix representations over one fixed field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A,B\in\mathbb F^{r\times E}\) be full-row-rank matrices whose columns share the same labels. They are projectively equivalent over \(\mathbb F\) if there exist \(P\in\operatorname{GL}_r(\mathbb F)\) and a nonsingular diagonal matrix \(D\in\mathbb F^{E\times E}\) such that
\[
B=PAD.
\]
Thus equivalence permits invertible row operations and independent nonzero scaling of columns, but no relabeling. Projectively equivalent matrices represent the same labeled matroid because these operations preserve all column-dependence relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two labeled representations are equivalent when invertible row operations and nonzero column scalings transform one into the other.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(B\) have full row rank over the same field.
Their columns have the same fixed labels.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B=PAD\implies M(B)=M(A).\)

notation.meaning: invertible r by r matrices over the field

review_flags: A source should confirm whether the intended convention also identifies field automorphisms.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated labeled projective-equivalence convention is coherent, but no source establishes that this leaf intends equivalence without relabeling or field automorphisms.

children.title: Reconstruction Uniqueness
children.top_down_role: Conditions governing canonical recovery or uniqueness up to accepted transformations.

knowledge_statements.title: Reconstruction Uniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniqueness relative to labeled projective equivalence over a fixed field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite \(\mathbb F\)-representable matroid \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) is uniquely representable over \(\mathbb F\) if any two full-row-rank \(\mathbb F\)-matrices \(A\) and \(B\), with columns labeled by \(E\) and satisfying \(M(A)=M(B)=M\), are projectively equivalent. Explicitly, uniqueness means that there exist \(P\in\operatorname{GL}_{r(M)}(\mathbb F)\) and a nonsingular diagonal matrix \(D\) such that \(B=PAD\). Hence any correct reconstruction determines one equivalence class, not necessarily one literal matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matroid is uniquely representable when all its labeled matrices over the field differ only by row operations and column scalings.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is finite and representable over \(\mathbb F\).
Representations use the same element labels.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall A,B:\ M(A)=M(B)=M\implies \exists P,D:\ B=PAD.\)
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports unique representability.

children.title: Representation Ambiguity
children.top_down_role: Nonuniqueness, incompatible reconstructions, plus field-sensitive ambiguity.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation Ambiguity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of reconstruction uniqueness over a fixed labeled field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Representation ambiguity occurs when a finite matroid \(M\) has two \(\mathbb F\)-representations \(A\) and \(B\) with the same labeled ground set but no matrices \(P\in\operatorname{GL}_{r(M)}(\mathbb F)\) and nonsingular diagonal \(D\) satisfy \(B=PAD\). In that case an independence oracle determines the matroid but does not determine a unique projective representation. For fields with suitable distinct cross-ratios, rank-two uniform matroids provide families of such inequivalent representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The same labeled matroid may have inequivalent matrix representations, so its independence data need not determine a unique reconstruction.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) has at least two representations over \(\mathbb F\).
Equivalence permits only row operations and nonzero column scalings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M(A)=M(B)=M\ \land\ \nexists P,D:\ B=PAD\implies M\text{ is not uniquely }\mathbb F\text{-representable}.\)
review_flags: The cross-ratio example requires a precise field-dependent source and formulation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-of-uniqueness criterion fits the failure-boundary leaf, but the cross-ratio example and its field conditions are too source-dependent to approve without a precise locator.

children.title: Matroid Structural Decomposition Theory
children.top_down_role: Classical structural theory retained at the level needed for representation, recognition, and algorithmic decomposition; enumerative and algebraic invariants are outside this chapter.

children.title: Connected Matroids
children.top_down_role: Structural features of connected matroids, including component boundaries relevant to decomposition.

knowledge_statements.title: Connected Matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Connectivity defined by absence of a nontrivial direct-sum separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M=(E,r)\) be a finite matroid with \(|E|\ge 2\), and define
\[
\lambda_M(X)=r(X)+r(E\setminus X)-r(E).
\]
The matroid \(M\) is connected if \(\lambda_M(X)>0\) for every nonempty proper subset \(X\subset E\). Equivalently, \(M\) admits no partition \(E=X\mathbin{\dot\cup}Y\) into nonempty sets with \(r(X)+r(Y)=r(E)\); equivalently, every pair of distinct elements belongs to a common circuit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matroid is connected when no nonempty partition separates its rank additively; equivalently, every two elements share a circuit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ connected}\iff \forall\varnothing\ne X\subsetneq E:\ \lambda_M(X)>0.\)

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

children.title: Two-Separations
children.top_down_role: Exact two-separation structure, crossing behavior, plus associated decomposition interfaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Two-Separations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard exact two-separation defined by the matroid connectivity function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M=(E,r)\) be a finite matroid. A two-separation of \(M\) is a partition \((X,E\setminus X)\) such that
\[
|X|\ge 2,\qquad |E\setminus X|\ge 2,\qquad \lambda_M(X)=1,
\]
where \(\lambda_M(X)=r(X)+r(E\setminus X)-r(E)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A two-separation partitions the ground set into two sides of size at least two whose ranks exceed the total rank by exactly one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((X,E\setminus X)\text{ is a two-separation}\iff |X|,|E\setminus X|\ge 2\ \land\ \lambda_M(X)=1.\)

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

children.title: One-Sum versus Two-Sum Boundaries
children.top_down_role: The transition from disconnected structure to connected but two-separable structure.

knowledge_statements.title: One-Sum versus Two-Sum Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank-connectivity boundary distinguishing direct-sum separations from two-separations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M=(E,r)\) be finite and let \(E=X\mathbin{\dot\cup}Y\) with \(X,Y\ne\varnothing\). The partition is a one-sum boundary exactly when
\[
\lambda_M(X)=0,
\]
in which case \(M=M|X\oplus M|Y\). If instead \(|X|,|Y|\ge2\) and \(\lambda_M(X)=1\), the partition is a two-separation. Thus connectivity excludes one-sum boundaries but does not exclude two-separations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Connectivity value zero gives a direct-sum split, whereas value one with both sides of size at least two defines a two-separation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_M(X)=0\iff M=M|X\oplus M|Y\), while \(|X|,|Y|\ge2\land\lambda_M(X)=1\) defines a two-separation.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

children.title: Three-Connected Matroids
children.top_down_role: Structural organization specific to the three-connected regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Three-Connected Matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite matroids, using the standard separation definition of 3-connectivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a finite matroid on a ground set \(E\) with rank function \(r\), and define \(\lambda_M(X)=r(X)+r(E\setminus X)-r(E)\). The matroid \(M\) is three-connected if \(|E|\ge 4\) and there is no partition \((X,E\setminus X)\) for which either \(|X|,|E\setminus X|\ge 1\) and \(\lambda_M(X)=0\), or \(|X|,|E\setminus X|\ge 2\) and \(\lambda_M(X)\le 1\). Thus a three-connected matroid has neither a 1-separation nor a 2-separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matroid is three-connected when it has at least four elements and admits neither a 1-separation nor a 2-separation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is three-connected}\iff M\text{ has no 1-separation or 2-separation}.\)

source_refs.locator: 5.2 Circuits and connectivity p. 176

source_witnesses.locator: 5.2 Circuits and connectivity p. 176

children.title: Higher-Order Connectivity
children.top_down_role: Connectivity levels beyond three-connectivity, with attention to their structural roles.

knowledge_statements.title: Higher-Order Connectivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite matroid \(k\)-connectivity defined by exclusion of all lower-order separations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(k\ge 2\), and let \(M\) be a finite matroid on \(E\) with \(|E|\ge 2(k-1)\). For \(1\le j<k\), a \(j\)-separation is a partition \((X,E\setminus X)\) satisfying \(|X|,|E\setminus X|\ge j\) and \(\lambda_M(X)\le j-1\). The matroid \(M\) is \(k\)-connected if it has no \(j\)-separation for any \(j<k\). Equivalently, every \(X\subseteq E\) with \(|X|,|E\setminus X|\ge j\) satisfies \(\lambda_M(X)\ge j\) for each \(1\le j<k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite matroid is k-connected when every separation of order below k is excluded, subject to the usual side-size requirements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is }k\text{-connected}\iff M\text{ has no }j\text{-separation for }1\le j<k.\)

source_refs.locator: 5.2 Circuits and connectivity p. 176

source_witnesses.locator: 5.2 Circuits and connectivity p. 176

children.title: Connectivity-Level Transitions
children.top_down_role: Boundaries between successive connectivity regimes under deletion, contraction, or decomposition.

knowledge_statements.title: Connectivity-Level Transitions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotonicity of the finite matroid connectivity hierarchy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(k\ge 2\), and let \(M\) be a finite matroid. Under the convention that \(q\)-connectivity excludes every \(j\)-separation with \(1\le j<q\), \((k+1)\)-connectivity implies \(k\)-connectivity. Thus the connectivity classes form a nested hierarchy. The reverse implication fails in general: a \(k\)-connected matroid possessing a \(k\)-separation is not \((k+1)\)-connected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every (k+1)-connected matroid is k-connected, while a k-connected matroid with a k-separation is not (k+1)-connected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is }(k+1)\text{-connected}\Longrightarrow M\text{ is }k\text{-connected}.\)

notation.meaning: a partition of order at most j with both sides of size at least j

source_refs.locator: 5.2 Circuits and connectivity p. 176

source_witnesses.locator: 5.2 Circuits and connectivity p. 176

children.title: Vertical Connectivity
children.top_down_role: Vertical separation structure plus its relation to rank-sensitive connectivity.

knowledge_statements.title: Vertical Connectivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank-based vertical connectivity for finite matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a finite matroid on \(E\). For an integer \(j\ge 1\), a vertical \(j\)-separation is a partition \((X,E\setminus X)\) such that \(\lambda_M(X)\le j-1\) and \(r(X),r(E\setminus X)\ge j\). For \(k\ge 2\), the matroid \(M\) is vertically \(k\)-connected if it has no vertical \(j\)-separation for any \(1\le j<k\). Unlike ordinary connectivity, the side constraints use rank rather than cardinality, so low-rank sides do not witness failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vertical k-connectivity excludes lower-order separations whose two sides both have sufficiently large rank.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is vertically }k\text{-connected}\iff M\text{ has no vertical }j\text{-separation for }1\le j<k.\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rank-based definition is plausible, but vertical-connectivity indexing and side-rank conventions vary. An authoritative source with a definition-level locator is required.

children.title: Cyclic Connectivity
children.top_down_role: Cyclic separation structure plus its dual interpretation.

knowledge_statements.title: Cyclic Connectivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-rank version of vertical connectivity for finite matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a finite matroid on \(E\), with dual rank function \(r^*\). For \(j\ge 1\), a cyclic \(j\)-separation is a partition \((X,E\setminus X)\) satisfying \(\lambda_M(X)\le j-1\) and \(r^*(X),r^*(E\setminus X)\ge j\). For \(k\ge 2\), the matroid \(M\) is cyclically \(k\)-connected if no cyclic \(j\)-separation exists for \(1\le j<k\). Equivalently, \(M\) is cyclically \(k\)-connected exactly when its dual \(M^*\) is vertically \(k\)-connected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cyclic k-connectivity is vertical k-connectivity in the dual matroid and uses dual ranks on both sides of a separation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is cyclically }k\text{-connected}\iff M^*\text{ is vertically }k\text{-connected}.\)

notation.meaning: rank function of the dual matroid

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed dual-rank definition is plausible, but the precise cyclic-connectivity convention and its equivalence with vertical connectivity of the dual require an authoritative source.

children.title: Local Connectivity
children.top_down_role: Connectivity measured between selected subsets or localized regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Connectivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank-theoretic local connectivity between two subsets of a matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M\) be a finite matroid with rank function \(r\), and let \(X,Y\subseteq E(M)\). The local connectivity of \(X\) and \(Y\) is
\[\sqcap_M(X,Y)=r(X)+r(Y)-r(X\cup Y).\]
It is symmetric and satisfies \(0\le \sqcap_M(X,Y)\le \min\{r(X),r(Y)\}\). If \(X\cap Y=\varnothing\), then \(\sqcap_M(X,Y)\) measures the rank lost when the two restrictions are combined; in particular, it is zero exactly when \(r(X\cup Y)=r(X)+r(Y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local connectivity is the rank overlap between two subsets, computed as the sum of their ranks minus the rank of their union.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sqcap_M(X,Y)=r(X)+r(Y)-r(X\cup Y).\)

notation.meaning: local connectivity of X and Y in M

source_refs.locator: 5.2 Circuits and connectivity p. 176

source_witnesses.locator: 5.2 Circuits and connectivity p. 176

children.title: Connectivity-Variant Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Implications, separations, plus dual correspondences among the named variants.

knowledge_statements.title: Connectivity-Variant Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Duality comparison among ordinary, vertical, and cyclic connectivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every finite matroid \(M\) and every \(X\subseteq E(M)\), duality preserves the connectivity function: \(\lambda_{M^*}(X)=\lambda_M(X)\). Consequently ordinary \(k\)-connectivity is self-dual. Because vertical separations impose rank constraints while cyclic separations impose the corresponding dual-rank constraints, a partition is a cyclic \(j\)-separation of \(M\) exactly when it is a vertical \(j\)-separation of \(M^*\). Therefore \(M\) is cyclically \(k\)-connected if and only if \(M^*\) is vertically \(k\)-connected, and conversely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ordinary connectivity is invariant under duality, while vertical and cyclic connectivity are exchanged by matroid duality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_{M^*}=\lambda_M,\qquad M\text{ cyclically }k\text{-connected}\iff M^*\text{ vertically }k\text{-connected}.\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The self-duality of the connectivity function and exchange of vertical and cyclic connectivity are standard-looking, but the exact convention-dependent claims have no cited source.

children.title: Matroid Connectivity Functions
children.top_down_role: Connectivity-function viewpoints used to organize separations across subsets.

knowledge_statements.title: Matroid Connectivity Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard normalized connectivity function of a finite matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M=(E,r)\) be a finite matroid. Its connectivity function is the integer-valued set function
\[\lambda_M(X)=r(X)+r(E\setminus X)-r(E),\qquad X\subseteq E.\]
It is normalized, symmetric, and submodular: \(\lambda_M(\varnothing)=0\), \(\lambda_M(X)=\lambda_M(E\setminus X)\), and
\[\lambda_M(X)+\lambda_M(Y)\ge \lambda_M(X\cap Y)+\lambda_M(X\cup Y)\]
for all \(X,Y\subseteq E\). Moreover, \(\lambda_M(X)\ge 0\), and its small values identify low-order separations of \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The matroid connectivity function measures rank interaction across a bipartition and is nonnegative, symmetric, normalized, and submodular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_M(X)=r(X)+r(E\setminus X)-r(E)\) is a normalized symmetric submodular function.

source_refs.locator: 5.2 Circuits and connectivity p. 176
1.2 Cut functions and connectivity concepts p. 19

source_witnesses.locator: 5.2 Circuits and connectivity p. 176
1.2 Cut functions and connectivity concepts p. 19

children.title: Matroid Branch-Width
children.top_down_role: Branch decompositions, width regimes, plus structural interpretations of bounded width.

knowledge_statements.title: Matroid Branch-Width
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Branch-width with edge width normalized as \(\lambda_M+1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a finite matroid on \(E\) with \(|E|\ge 2\). A branch-decomposition is a pair \((T,\tau)\), where \(T\) is a tree whose internal vertices have degree three and \(\tau:E\to L(T)\) is a bijection. Each edge \(e\in E(T)\) determines a bipartition \((A_e,E\setminus A_e)\) from the two components of \(T-e\). Its width is \(\lambda_M(A_e)+1\). The width of \((T,\tau)\) is the maximum edge width, and the branch-width \(\operatorname{bw}(M)\) is the minimum such width over all branch-decompositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matroid branch-width minimizes the largest connectivity value, plus one, displayed by an edge of a subcubic leaf-labeled tree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{bw}(M)=\min_{(T,\tau)}\max_{e\in E(T)}\bigl(\lambda_M(A_e)+1\bigr).\)

notation.meaning: one side of the bipartition displayed by tree edge e

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is coherent, but matroid branch-width conventions differ by a plus-one shift. The selected normalization requires an authoritative definition-level citation.

children.title: Branch-Width via Connectivity Functions
children.top_down_role: How connectivity measurements induce width evaluations on branch decompositions.

knowledge_statements.title: Branch-Width via Connectivity Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Branch-width as the decomposition width induced by a connectivity function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E\) be finite and let \(f:2^E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\) be symmetric. For a branch-decomposition \((T,\tau)\), define
\[w_f(T,\tau)=\max_{e\in E(T)} f(A_e),\qquad \operatorname{bw}(f)=\min_{(T,\tau)}w_f(T,\tau).\]
For a matroid \(M	o E\), use the shifted connectivity function \(f_M(X)=\lambda_M(X)+1\). Then matroid branch-width is exactly the branch-width of this connectivity system:
\[\operatorname{bw}(M)=\operatorname{bw}(f_M)=\min_{(T,\tau)}\max_{e\in E(T)}\bigl(\lambda_M(A_e)+1\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matroid branch-width is precisely the branch-decomposition width of its connectivity function under the stated plus-one normalization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{bw}(M)=\operatorname{bw}(\lambda_M+1).\)

notation.meaning: shifted connectivity function defined by lambda plus one
side displayed by a decomposition-tree edge
branch-width induced by symmetric function f

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The connectivity-function representation and plus-one normalization require a source. In addition, “M\to E” is malformed and should read that M is a matroid on E once the sourced convention is established.

children.title: Bounded-Width Structural Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural consequences plus algorithmic interfaces associated with bounded branch-width.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Width Structural Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A branch-decomposition as a certificate of bounded matroid branch-width.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M=(E,r)\) be a finite matroid and let \(b\ge 1\). A branch-decomposition \((T,\tau)\) certifies \(\operatorname{bw}(M)\le b\) if every edge \(e\in E(T)\), displaying \((A_e,E\setminus A_e)\), satisfies
\[r(A_e)+r(E\setminus A_e)-r(E)+1\le b.\]
The certificate is checked by verifying that \(T\) is subcubic, \(\tau\) bijects \(E\) with its leaves, and the displayed inequality holds for every tree edge. Existence of such a certificate is equivalent to membership in the branch-width-at-most-\(b\) regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subcubic leaf-labeled tree certifies branch-width at most b when every displayed matroid separation has width at most b.
assumptions_latex: Rank values for displayed subsets are available for verification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{bw}(M)\le b\iff \exists(T,\tau)\ \forall e\in E(T):\lambda_M(A_e)+1\le b.\)

notation.meaning: side displayed by tree edge e

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A displayed branch-decomposition is a suitable certificate for the bounded-width leaf, but the normalization and rank-access verification model depend on the unsourced branch-width convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Tutte Linking Theory
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-matroid linking theorem for two disjoint terminal sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M\) be a finite matroid on \(E\), and let \(S,T\subseteq E\) be disjoint. Define
\[\kappa_M(S,T)=\min\{\lambda_M(X):S\subseteq X\subseteq E\setminus T\}.\]
There is a partition \((C,D)\) of \(E\setminus(S\cup T)\) such that the minor \(N=M/C\setminus D\), whose ground set is \(S\cup T\), satisfies \(N|S=M|S\), \(N|T=M|T\), and
\[\kappa_N(S,T)=\kappa_M(S,T).\]
Thus all nonterminal elements can be contracted or deleted while preserving both terminal restrictions and their minimum separation order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tutte's linking theorem produces a minor on two terminal sets that preserves their restrictions and minimum connectivity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists C\mathbin{\dot\cup}D=E\setminus(S\cup T):\ N=M/C\setminus D,\ \kappa_N(S,T)=\kappa_M(S,T),\ N|S=M|S,\ N|T=M|T.\)

notation.meaning: minimum connectivity separating S from T
minor formed by contracting C and deleting D

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is an appropriate theorem for Tutte linking theory, but the exact minor conclusion, preservation of both terminal restrictions, and connectivity normalization require an authoritative theorem-level citation.

children.title: Wheel Matroids
children.top_down_role: Wheel structure within highly connected matroids plus its splitter-theoretic role.

knowledge_statements.title: Wheel Matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the finite rank-wheel matroid as the cycle matroid of a wheel graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an integer \(r\ge 3\), let \(W_r\) be the graph obtained from a cycle \(v_1v_2\cdots v_rv_1\) by adjoining a hub \(h\) and the spokes \(hv_i\) for \(1\le i\le r\). The rank-\(r\) wheel matroid is the cycle matroid \(M(W_r)\). Its ground set comprises the \(r\) rim edges and \(r\) spokes, and its bases are precisely the edge sets of spanning trees of \(W_r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A wheel matroid is the cycle matroid of a cycle joined to a central hub; its bases are the wheel graph's spanning trees.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M(W_r)\) is a rank-\(r\) graphic matroid on \(2r\) elements.

notation.meaning: wheel graph with r rim vertices and one hub
cycle matroid of a graph G

review_flags: Exact supporting definition locator is absent from the supplied source inventory.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition, content kind, notation, and rank/ground-set claims are mathematically standard and fit the Wheel Matroids leaf, but no citation or inspectable locator supports the record. A source specifically defining wheel matroids is required.

children.title: Whirl Matroids
children.top_down_role: Whirl structure, representability regimes, plus contrasts with wheels.

knowledge_statements.title: Whirl Matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the standard relaxation definition of a finite whirl.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M(W_r)\) be the rank-\(r\) wheel matroid for \(r\ge 3\), and let \(R\) be its set of rim edges. The set \(R\) is a circuit-hyperplane of \(M(W_r)\). The rank-\(r\) whirl \(\mathcal W^r\) is the relaxation of \(R\): its collection of bases is \[\mathcal B(\mathcal W^r)=\mathcal B(M(W_r))\cup\{R\}.\] Thus the relaxation makes the rim a basis while leaving every former wheel basis unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rank-r whirl is obtained from the rank-r wheel matroid by relaxing its rim circuit-hyperplane, thereby declaring the rim to be a basis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal W^r\) is the rank-\(r\) relaxation of \(M(W_r)\) at its rim.
review_flags: Exact supporting definition locator is absent from the supplied source inventory.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The relaxation definition is standard and fits the Whirl Matroids leaf, but the record supplies no source for the rim circuit-hyperplane claim or the stated basis description of the relaxation.

children.title: Deletion–Contraction Fragility
children.top_down_role: Elements whose deletion or contraction disrupts the required connectivity regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Deletion–Contraction Fragility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines fragility relative to a fixed minor in finite matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) and \(N\) be finite matroids. The matroid \(M\) is \(N\)-fragile if \(N\) is a minor of \(M\) and, for every \(e\in E(M)\), at most one of \(M\backslash e\) and \(M/e\) has an \(N\)-minor. Equivalently, no element is simultaneously deletable and contractible while preserving an \(N\)-minor. An element may nevertheless be essential, meaning that neither operation preserves such a minor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matroid is N-fragile when it has an N-minor but no element can be both deleted and contracted while retaining an N-minor.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is }N\text{-fragile}\iff N\preccurlyeq M\text{ and }\forall e\in E(M),\;\neg(N\preccurlyeq M\backslash e\text{ and }N\preccurlyeq M/e)\).

notation.meaning: N is isomorphic to a minor of M

review_flags: Terminology varies between fragile and strictly fragile; an exact source is required to certify this convention.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement coherently defines fragility as absence of N-flexible elements and correctly distinguishes essential elements, but published conventions differ between N-fragile and strictly N-fragile. An exact definition locator is required before selecting this convention.

children.title: Wheel–Whirl Exceptional Regimes
children.top_down_role: Exceptional cases where ordinary splitter extensions require separate treatment.

knowledge_statements.title: Wheel–Whirl Exceptional Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records why wheels and whirls require exceptions in literal splitter statements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(r\ge 3\), let \(M\) be the wheel \(M(W_r)\) or the whirl \(\mathcal W^r\). For every \(e\in E(M)\), neither \(M\backslash e\) nor \(M/e\) is 3-connected: one operation exposes a series class and the dual operation exposes a parallel class. Consequently, a splitter assertion demanding a proper 3-connected single-element deletion or contraction cannot be applied literally within a wheel or whirl chain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every single deletion or contraction of a wheel or whirl destroys 3-connectivity, so literal one-element splitter conclusions need an exceptional clause.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall e\in E(M),\;M\backslash e\text{ and }M/e\text{ are not 3-connected}\).
review_flags: A precise wheel–whirl splitter-exception locator is not supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary content kind fits the leaf and the claim is consistent with the standard wheel-whirl obstruction, but no source verifies the universal deletion/contraction statement, including its asserted series/parallel behavior for all ranks covered.

children.title: Classical Splitter Regime
children.top_down_role: Scope, hypotheses, plus structural reach of the classical splitter result.

knowledge_statements.title: Classical Splitter Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-matroid form of the classical Splitter Theorem with the wheel–whirl proviso.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) and \(N\) be 3-connected finite matroids such that \(N\) is a proper minor of \(M\) and \(|E(N)|\ge 4\). If \(N\) is a wheel or whirl, additionally suppose that \(M\) has no wheel or whirl minor, respectively, with more elements than \(N\). Then some \(e\in E(M)\) satisfies one of the following: \(M\backslash e\) is 3-connected and has an \(N\)-minor, or \(M/e\) is 3-connected and has an \(N\)-minor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outside the stated wheel–whirl obstruction, a proper 3-connected minor can be retained after a deletion or contraction that preserves 3-connectivity.
assumptions_latex: \(N\) is a proper minor of \(M\) and \(|E(N)|\ge 4\)
The wheel–whirl maximality proviso holds when applicable
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists e\in E(M)\) such that \((N\preccurlyeq M\backslash e\text{ and }M\backslash e\text{ is 3-connected})\) or \((N\preccurlyeq M/e\text{ and }M/e\text{ is 3-connected})\).

notation.meaning: N is isomorphic to a minor of M

review_flags: The supplied inventory contains no exact Splitter Theorem locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is appropriately classified as a theorem and resembles the classical Splitter Theorem, but the precise wheel-whirl maximality proviso and the size hypotheses vary among formulations. No exact theorem locator is supplied, so the hypotheses and conclusion cannot be certified.

children.title: Constructive Splitter Sequences
children.top_down_role: Extension or coextension sequences used to navigate between connected minors.

knowledge_statements.title: Constructive Splitter Sequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iterated sequence form of the classical splitter conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the classical Splitter Theorem hypotheses, there is a sequence \(N=M_0,M_1,\ldots,M_k=M\) of 3-connected matroids such that each \(M_i\) is a minor of \(M\) and \(|E(M_i)|=|E(N)|+i\). For every \(i<k\), the matroid \(M_{i+1}\) is a single-element extension or single-element coextension of \(M_i\). Equivalently, deleting or contracting the newly added element of \(M_{i+1}\) recovers \(M_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The splitter theorem can be iterated into a chain from N to M whose 3-connected members differ by one extension or coextension.
assumptions_latex: The hypotheses of the classical Splitter Theorem hold for \(M\) and \(N\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N=M_0\prec M_1\prec\cdots\prec M_k=M\), with every \(M_i\) 3-connected and \(|E(M_{i+1})\setminus E(M_i)|=1\).

notation.meaning: the ground-set size difference between M and N

review_flags: The sequence formulation requires an exact splitter-theorem source locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A sequence representation fits the leaf, but an exact source is needed to justify iteration of the splitter conclusion through every intermediate matroid. The conclusion also uses the undefined relation symbol \(\prec\) and literal ground-set differences despite the statement formulating the objects only as minors up to isomorphism.

children.title: Strengthened Splitter Variants
children.top_down_role: Variants imposing stronger connectivity, representation, or sequence-control requirements.

knowledge_statements.title: Strengthened Splitter Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong sequence form controlling consecutive extensions and coextensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the classical splitter hypotheses, the 3-connected sequence from \(N\) to \(M\) can, after dualizing if necessary, be chosen in blocks containing at most two consecutive single-element extensions followed by at most one single-element coextension. Whenever a block adds two extension elements and then one coextension element, its three new elements form a triad in the matroid at the end of that block. Thus both intermediate size and the local configuration of added elements are controlled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strong splitter sequence can bound consecutive extensions and coextensions; a maximal three-element block creates a triad.
assumptions_latex: The classical splitter hypotheses hold for \(M\) and \(N\)
Dualization of the sequence is allowed
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sequence may be ordered into extension–coextension blocks of size at most \(3\), with every size-\(3\) block's new elements forming a triad.
review_flags: Strong Splitter Theorem formulations have technical size and ordering conventions that require source verification.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem content kind fits the strengthened-variant leaf, but strong splitter theorems have formulation-sensitive ordering, fan/triad, size, and exception hypotheses. The informal block formulation cannot be certified without a specific theorem citation.

children.title: Splitter Exceptions
children.top_down_role: Exceptional classes plus boundary cases requiring modified splitter conclusions.

knowledge_statements.title: Splitter Exceptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nested wheels and whirls refute the splitter conclusion without its exceptional proviso.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(r\ge 3\), the rank-\(r\) wheel \(M(W_r)\) is a proper minor of \(M(W_{r+1})\), and the rank-\(r\) whirl \(\mathcal W^r\) is a proper minor of \(\mathcal W^{r+1}\). Nevertheless, for every element \(e\) of the larger matroid, both its deletion and contraction fail to be 3-connected. Hence omitting the wheel–whirl maximality proviso makes the literal single-element conclusion of the classical Splitter Theorem false.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Consecutive wheels or whirls form nested 3-connected minors, yet no deletion or contraction of the larger member remains 3-connected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pairs \((M(W_{r+1}),M(W_r))\) and \((\mathcal W^{r+1},\mathcal W^r)\) violate the unqualified splitter conclusion.
review_flags: The nested-minor construction and exception require an exact source locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample content kind fits Splitter Exceptions, and the proposed wheel-whirl pairs express the intended obstruction. A precise source is still required for both the nested-minor assertions and the universal failure of 3-connectivity after either single-element operation.

children.title: Graphic Excluded Minors
children.top_down_role: Minor-minimal obstructions to graphic structure plus their recognition role.

knowledge_statements.title: Graphic Excluded Minors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tutte's excluded-minor characterization of finite graphic matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite matroid \(M\) is graphic if and only if it has no minor isomorphic to any member of \[\{U_{2,4},F_7,F_7^*,M^*(K_5),M^*(K_{3,3})\}.\] Each listed matroid is nongraphic, while every proper minor of it is graphic; consequently these five matroids are precisely the excluded minors for the minor-closed class of finite graphic matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite matroid is graphic exactly when it excludes U(2,4), the two Fano matroids, and the cographic matroids of K5 and K3,3.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is graphic}\iff M\text{ has no minor in }\{U_{2,4},F_7,F_7^*,M^*(K_5),M^*(K_{3,3})\}\).

notation.meaning: dual of the cycle matroid of G
rank-2 uniform matroid on four elements

review_flags: No supplied locator identifies Tutte's exact graphic excluded-minor theorem.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The five-obstruction characterization is the standard finite graphic excluded-minor theorem and the theorem content kind fits the leaf, but the candidate provides no citation or theorem/page locator.

children.title: Cographic Excluded Minors
children.top_down_role: Minor-minimal obstructions to cographic structure viewed through duality.

knowledge_statements.title: Cographic Excluded Minors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual form of the finite graphic excluded-minor characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite matroid \(M\) is cographic if and only if it has no minor isomorphic to any member of \[\{U_{2,4},F_7,F_7^*,M(K_5),M(K_{3,3})\}.\] This follows under matroid duality because deletion and contraction are interchanged, \(U_{2,4}\) is self-dual, \(F_7\) and \(F_7^*\) are dual, and \(M^*(G)^*=M(G)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite matroid is cographic exactly when it excludes U(2,4), both Fano matroids, and the cycle matroids of K5 and K3,3.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is cographic}\iff M\text{ has no minor in }\{U_{2,4},F_7,F_7^*,M(K_5),M(K_{3,3})\}\).

notation.meaning: rank-2 uniform matroid on four elements

review_flags: No supplied locator identifies the exact cographic excluded-minor characterization.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated obstruction family is the expected dual of the finite graphic excluded-minor family and fits the cographic leaf, but neither the underlying theorem nor its dual formulation has an inspectable citation.

children.title: Regular Excluded Minors
children.top_down_role: Minor-minimal obstructions separating regular matroids from broader representable classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Regular Excluded Minors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tutte's excluded-minor characterization of finite regular matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite matroid \(M\) is regular—that is, representable over every field—if and only if it has no minor isomorphic to \(U_{2,4}\), \(F_7\), or \(F_7^*\). Equivalently, regularity is characterized among finite matroids by binary representability together with exclusion of the Fano matroid and its dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite matroid is regular exactly when it has no U(2,4), Fano, or dual-Fano minor.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is regular}\iff M\text{ has no minor isomorphic to }U_{2,4},F_7,\text{ or }F_7^*\).

notation.meaning: rank-2 uniform matroid on four elements

review_flags: No supplied locator identifies Tutte's exact regular-matroid theorem.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The excluded-minor characterization of finite regular matroids is standard and correctly classified as a theorem, but no exact source locator is supplied for either the three-obstruction form or its binary reformulation.

children.title: Duality across Obstruction Families
children.top_down_role: Dual correspondences plus containment relationships among the obstruction families.

knowledge_statements.title: Duality across Obstruction Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes how excluded-minor families transform under matroid duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal C\) be a minor-closed class of finite matroids, and define \(\mathcal C^*=\{M^*:M\in\mathcal C\}\). If \(\operatorname{Ex}(\mathcal C)\) denotes the excluded minors for \(\mathcal C\), then \[\operatorname{Ex}(\mathcal C^*)=\{X^*:X\in\operatorname{Ex}(\mathcal C)\}.\] Hence graphic and cographic obstruction families are dual, while the regular obstruction family is closed under duality because \(U_{2,4}\) is self-dual and \(F_7^*=F_7^*\) pairs with \(F_7\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dualizing a minor-closed class dualizes every excluded minor; graphic and cographic obstructions correspond, while regular obstructions are duality-invariant.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal C\) is a minor-closed class of finite matroids
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Ex}(\mathcal C^*)=\operatorname{Ex}(\mathcal C)^*\).

notation.meaning: class consisting of duals of members of C

review_flags: The supplied inventory lacks an exact locator for excluded-minor duality.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The duality content kind and excluded-minor transformation formula fit the leaf, but no citation supports the general claim. The final clause also contains the tautological wording \(F_7^*=F_7^*\); it should instead state that \(F_7\) and \(F_7^*\) form a dual pair once a source is supplied.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is a finite family \(\mathcal{X}_q\) such that \(M\) is representable over \(\operatorname{GF}(q)\) if and only if no minor of \(M\) is isomorphic to a member of \(\mathcal{X}_q\).

notation.meaning: the finite field with q elements

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-matroid form of the fixed-finite-field excluded-minor theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every prime power \(q\), there exists a finite set \(\mathcal{X}_q\) of finite matroids such that a finite matroid \(M\) is representable over \(\operatorname{GF}(q)\) exactly when no minor of \(M\) is isomorphic to an element of \(\mathcal{X}_q\). The family may be chosen as the excluded minors: every \(N\in\mathcal{X}_q\) is not representable over \(\operatorname{GF}(q)\), while every proper minor of \(N\) is representable over \(\operatorname{GF}(q)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each finite field, representability is characterized by avoiding a finite collection of excluded minors.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Field Excluded-Minor Programs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fixed-field excluded-minor theorem is stated precisely and the theorem kind fits, but no citation supports this deep result.

children.title: Graphic Decomposition Pieces
children.top_down_role: Graphic building blocks appearing in regular-matroid decompositions.

assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite graph, with loops and parallel edges permitted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A regular-matroid decomposition leaf is graphic when it is isomorphic to \(M(G)\) for some finite graph \(G\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graphic leaves in a regular-matroid decomposition.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The graphic matroid of a finite graph \(G\) is the matroid \(M(G)\) on \(E(G)\) whose independent sets are precisely the edge sets containing no graph cycle. Equivalently, its circuits are the edge sets of graph cycles, including a loop as a one-edge cycle and a parallel pair as a two-edge cycle. A graphic decomposition piece is a matroid isomorphic to \(M(G)\) for some \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graphic piece is a cycle matroid: its independent sets are forests and its circuits are graph cycles.
knowledge_statements.title: Graphic Decomposition Pieces

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

children.title: Cographic Decomposition Pieces
children.top_down_role: Cographic building blocks appearing through dual graphic structure.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A regular-matroid decomposition leaf is cographic when it is isomorphic to \(M(G)^*\) for some finite graph \(G\).

notation.meaning: the bond matroid, dual to the cycle matroid of G

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cographic leaves in a regular-matroid decomposition.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The cographic matroid associated with a finite graph \(G\) is the dual \(M(G)^*\) of its cycle matroid. Its circuits are exactly the bonds of \(G\), namely the inclusion-minimal nonempty edge cuts. A cographic decomposition piece is a matroid isomorphic to \(M(G)^*\) for some \(G\); equivalently, it is the dual of a graphic matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cographic piece is dual to a cycle matroid, and its circuits are the graph's minimal nonempty cuts.
knowledge_statements.title: Cographic Decomposition Pieces

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

children.title: Sporadic Decomposition Pieces
children.top_down_role: Exceptional finite building blocks outside the graphic or cographic families.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sporadic leaf type in Seymour's regular-matroid decomposition is the matroid \(R_{10}\).

notation.meaning: the ten-element rank-five sporadic regular matroid

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The exceptional leaf type in the regular-matroid decomposition theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(R_{10}\) as the binary vector matroid represented by the \(5\times 10\) matrix \([I_5\mid J_5-I_5]\) over \(\operatorname{GF}(2)\). It is a ten-element rank-five regular matroid that is neither graphic nor cographic. In the piece taxonomy for regular-matroid decomposition, the sporadic pieces are precisely leaves isomorphic to \(R_{10}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sole sporadic leaf type is the ten-element rank-five regular matroid R10, which is neither graphic nor cographic.
knowledge_statements.title: Sporadic Decomposition Pieces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The R10 representation and its role as Seymour's exceptional piece require an inspectable authoritative source; none is cited.

children.title: Piece-Type Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Compatibility boundaries governing how distinct piece types participate in a decomposition.

assumptions_latex: \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are binary matroids with identified overlap \(T=E(M_1)\cap E(M_2)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The interface is deleted after gluing, so the recomposed ground set is \((E(M_1)\cup E(M_2))\setminus T\).

notation.meaning: a k-sum of the two pieces

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interface sizes and deletion convention for binary 1-, 2-, and 3-sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the binary-sum representation of a decomposition edge, a \(1\)-sum has \(T=\varnothing\), a \(2\)-sum uses an identified one-element set \(T\), and a \(3\)-sum uses an identified three-element set \(T\). For a proper \(2\)-sum the interface element is neither a loop nor a coloop in either piece. For a proper binary \(3\)-sum, \(T\) is a circuit in each piece and contains no cocircuit of either piece. The interface elements are auxiliary and are deleted from the recomposed matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Decomposition edges carry empty, one-element, or three-element interfaces, with nondegeneracy conditions and deletion after gluing.
knowledge_statements.title: Piece-Type Interfaces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Interface sizes, nondegeneracy predicates, and deletion conventions vary among formulations and require a cited primary convention.

children.title: Binary Three-Sums
children.top_down_role: Binary three-sum structure plus its role in regular-matroid decomposition.

assumptions_latex: \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are binary matroids with \(E(M_1)\cap E(M_2)=T\).
\(T\) has three elements, is a circuit of each matroid, and contains no cocircuit of either.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The specified cycle family determines the binary three-sum \(M_1\oplus_3 M_2\) on \((E(M_1)\cup E(M_2))\setminus T\).

notation.meaning: the family of cycles of M

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cycle-space definition of a proper binary three-sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The binary three-sum \(M=M_1\oplus_3 M_2\) has ground set \((E(M_1)\cup E(M_2))\setminus T\). Its cycles are the sets
\[
\mathcal{Z}(M)=\{Z_1\triangle Z_2: Z_i\in\mathcal{Z}(M_i),\ Z_1\cap T=Z_2\cap T\}.
\]
Because the traces on \(T\) agree, every displayed symmetric difference avoids \(T\). The resulting family is a binary cycle space and therefore determines a binary matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary three-sum matches the two cycle spaces along a common triangle and then removes that triangle.
knowledge_statements.title: Binary Three-Sums

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cycle-space formula is plausible and well formed, but its hypotheses and exact binary three-sum convention are unsupported by a citation.

children.title: Three-Sum Recomposition
children.top_down_role: Recovery of a global matroid from compatible decomposition pieces.

assumptions_latex: A rooted binary tree has leaf matroids and internal nodes labeled by valid binary \(1\)-, \(2\)-, or \(3\)-sum interfaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The matroid stored at the root is the recomposition represented by the entire decomposition tree.

notation.meaning: the matroid recomposed at tree node v
the sum type labeling an internal node

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bottom-up recomposition of a binary decomposition tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize each leaf \(v\) with its supplied matroid \(M_v\). Process internal nodes in postorder. If \(v\) has children \(a,b\), validate their identified interface and set \(M_v=M_a\oplus_{k_v}M_b\), deleting the interface elements according to the chosen sum convention. Stop after processing the root \(r\), and output \(M_r\). If any interface fails its size, circuit, cocircuit, or element-identification conditions, output an invalid-decomposition report instead of a matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recompose a decomposition tree bottom-up, validating each interface and applying its indicated one-, two-, or three-sum.
knowledge_statements.title: Three-Sum Recomposition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits recomposition, but correctness depends on exact sum conventions and interface-validation rules for which no source is supplied.

children.title: Three-Sum Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Boundary data controlling which decomposition pieces can be recomposed.

assumptions_latex: \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are binary matroids and \(T=E(M_1)\cap E(M_2)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under these predicates, the cycle-space gluing along \(T\) defines a proper binary three-sum.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility predicate for a proper binary three-sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The pieces are three-sum compatible when \(|T|=3\); the restrictions of their labels to \(T\) identify the same three elements; \(T\) is a circuit of both \(M_1\) and \(M_2\); and no cocircuit of either matroid is contained in \(T\). Equivalently, \(T\) contains no circuit of \(M_1^*\) or \(M_2^*\). A proper-sum convention may additionally require each piece to retain sufficiently many elements outside \(T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Three-sum compatibility requires a consistently identified common triangle that contains no cocircuit of either piece.
knowledge_statements.title: Three-Sum Compatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The compatibility conditions are convention-sensitive, and the phrase 'sufficiently many elements' leaves a possible properness hypothesis unspecified.

children.title: Recomposition Ambiguity
children.top_down_role: Noncanonical decomposition trees, equivalent recompositions, plus exceptional overlaps.

assumptions_latex: \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) have a compatible three-element interface \(T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Interface maps differing by \(\phi|_T\) can encode isomorphic recomposed matroids, so decomposition data are not uniquely recoverable from the result.

notation.meaning: an automorphism of the second piece

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonuniqueness caused by interface symmetries and alternative separation choices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an interface identification \(f:T\to T\) glues \(M_1\) to \(M_2\). Replacing it by \(\phi|_T\circ f\) changes the labeled gluing data whenever \(\phi|_T\) is nontrivial, but applying \(\phi\) on the second piece induces an isomorphism between the two recomposed matroids. Thus a recomposed matroid need not determine its interface identification. More generally, choosing different valid three-separations can yield nonisomorphic decomposition trees with isomorphic roots.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interface symmetries or different three-separations can produce distinct decomposition descriptions of the same matroid.
knowledge_statements.title: Recomposition Ambiguity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The automorphism argument is plausible, but the labeled-versus-unlabeled convention and broader claim about nonunique decomposition trees need a source or explicit example.

children.title: Recognition from Decomposition
children.top_down_role: Recognition organized through basic pieces plus decomposition certificates.

assumptions_latex: A supplied tree has graphic, cographic, or \(R_{10}\) leaves and valid \(1\)-, \(2\)-, or \(3\)-sum nodes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The validated tree certifies that \(M\) is regular; conversely, every regular matroid admits such a tree.

notation.meaning: the recomposed matroid at node v

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural recognition certificate based on Seymour decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Verify each leaf as graphic, cographic, or isomorphic to \(R_{10}\). At every internal node, verify the stated interface conditions and that its stored matroid equals the indicated \(1\)-, \(2\)-, or \(3\)-sum of its children. Finally verify that the root is isomorphic to \(M\). Since the three leaf classes are regular and regularity is preserved by these sums, the tree certifies regularity. Seymour's decomposition theorem supplies the converse existence statement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid tree of graphic, cographic, and R10 pieces certifies regularity, and every regular matroid has such a tree.
knowledge_statements.title: Recognition from Decomposition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind fits recognition from decomposition, but both preservation under the stated sums and the converse decomposition theorem require authoritative support.

children.title: Optimization over Decomposition Trees
children.top_down_role: Optimization interfaces that combine solutions across a decomposition tree.

assumptions_latex: A rooted decomposition tree represents a binary matroid, and every parent-child interface has at most three elements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The root table yields the maximum weight of an independent set and backtracking yields an optimizer.

notation.meaning: the rank-marginal signature of I on interface T
the best weight at node v with signature sigma

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-interface dynamic programming for maximum-weight independence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each node \(v\), each independent set \(I\) in its submatroid induces the interface signature \(\sigma_I(X)=r(I\cup X)-r(I)\) for every \(X\subseteq T_v\). At a leaf, compute \(F_v(\sigma)=\max\{w(I):I\text{ is independent and has signature }\sigma\}\). At an internal node, enumerate pairs of child signatures compatible with its sum, combine their values while subtracting any counted interface contribution, and retain the maximum for each parent signature. Output the unrestricted optimum at the root and recover a maximizing set by stored back-pointers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dynamic programming records each partial independent set's rank behavior on the small interface and combines compatible child states.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimization over Decomposition Trees

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source establishes that the proposed rank-marginal signature is sufficient to combine independent-set solutions across every permitted interface.

children.title: Piecewise Certificate Transfer
children.top_down_role: Transfer of local recognition or optimization certificates to the recomposed matroid.

assumptions_latex: Every leaf supplies a locally checkable certificate and every internal sum supplies its interface map.
The certified property is preserved by each permitted sum when the interface predicates hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The collection of leaf certificates, interface checks, and bottom-up transfer records is a certificate for the root property.

notation.meaning: a certificate attached to tree node v
the matroid represented at tree node v
the interface at an internal node v

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compositional certificate schema for properties preserved by matroid sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Attach to each leaf \(v\) a certificate \(C_v\) verifiable directly for \(M_v\). For an internal node \(v\) with children \(a,b\), verify the interface \(T_v\), verify that \(M_v=M_a\oplus_{k_v}M_b\), and apply the property's stated transfer rule to \(C_a,C_b\) to construct \(C_v\). A verifier processes the tree in postorder and accepts only if every local certificate, interface predicate, and transfer step succeeds. The resulting root object \(C_r\) certifies the property for \(M_r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Leaf certificates transfer to the root when every interface is valid and the certified property is preserved by each sum.
knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise Certificate Transfer

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is only an abstract conditional schema; a specific certified property, local verifier, and sum-preservation theorem are needed to make the certificate claim substantive.

children.title: Decomposition Overheads
children.top_down_role: Costs caused by finding, representing, traversing, or recomposing decomposition pieces.

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition Overheads
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ground-set duplication overhead in a bounded-adhesion regular-matroid decomposition tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) have \(n\) elements and be represented by a tree \(T\) of \(t\) pieces combined by 1-, 2-, or 3-sums. Suppose every tree edge has an adhesion set of size at most \(3\), stored in both incident pieces, and reconstruction deletes the copied adhesion elements. Then the aggregate number of stored ground-set incidences is at most \(n+6(t-1)\). Consequently, tree navigation and interface storage require \(O(t)\) additional space, while scanning all explicitly stored pieces requires \(O(n+t)\) time, excluding decomposition construction and piece-local optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded-adhesion decomposition duplicates only constantly many elements per tree edge, so explicit piece storage and traversal add linear overhead.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is a finite tree of 1-, 2-, or 3-sum pieces.
Each adhesion set has cardinality at most \(3\).
Each adhesion element is stored at most once at each endpoint of its tree edge.

notation.meaning: stored ground set of the piece at node v

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bound depends on the precise conventions for 1-, 2-, and 3-sum interfaces, copied adhesion elements, and deletion during reconstruction. No source is supplied, so the exact coefficient and accounting model cannot be validated reliably.

children.title: Matroid Computational Model Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Computational interfaces precede algorithm branches so complexity claims are interpreted in the appropriate oracle or explicit-representation model.

children.title: Independence Oracles
children.top_down_role: Information access, query costs, plus certifying limits for independence queries.

knowledge_statements.title: Independence Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boolean independence-query model for a finite matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite matroid \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\), an independence oracle is a procedure \(\mathcal O_{\mathrm{ind}}\) that accepts any subset \(X\subseteq E\) and returns \(1\) exactly when \(X\in\mathcal I\), and returns \(0\) otherwise. Oracle complexity counts calls to \(\mathcal O_{\mathrm{ind}}\) separately from ordinary computation and from the cost of encoding or reading subsets of \(E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An independence oracle answers whether a queried subset of the ground set is independent in the matroid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal O_{\mathrm{ind}}(X)=1\iff X\in\mathcal I\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Best-In Greedy Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tie ordering among equally weighted elements may be arbitrary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite independence system $(E,\mathcal F)$ through an independence oracle and weights $c:E\to\mathbb R_+$, order $E=\{e_1,\ldots,e_n\}$ so that $c(e_1)\geq\cdots\geq c(e_n)$. Initialize $F:=\varnothing$ and, for $i=1,\ldots,n$, replace $F$ by $F\cup\{e_i\}$ whenever $F\cup\{e_i\}\in\mathcal F$. Return $F$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Process the elements in nonincreasing weight order, adding an element exactly when independence is preserved, and return the resulting feasible set.
assumptions_latex: (E,\mathcal F)\text{ is a finite independence system}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\in\mathcal F
