children.title: Base-Polytope Duality
children.top_down_role: Geometric correspondence between primal-base structure plus dual-matroid base structure.

assumptions_latex: \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) is a finite matroid with rank function \(r_M\).
\(M^*\) denotes the dual matroid and \(\mathbf1\in\mathbb R^E\) is the all-ones vector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[B(M^*)=\mathbf1-B(M),\qquad r_{M^*}(S)=|S|-r_M(E)+r_M(E\setminus S).\]

notation.meaning: Affine reflection of a set P.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine complement duality for finite matroid base polytopes.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172
1.7 The Matroid Polytope p. 66
source_refs.source_title: A First Course in Combinatorial Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A set \(B\subseteq E\) is a base of \(M\) if and only if \(E\setminus B\) is a base of \(M^*\). Therefore complementation of incidence vectors gives the affine identity
\[B(M^*)=\{\mathbf1-x:x\in B(M)\}=\mathbf1-B(M).\]
The compatible rank transformation is
\[r_{M^*}(S)=|S|-r_M(E)+r_M(E\setminus S)\qquad(S\subseteq E).\]
Consequently, maximizing \(w^\top x\) over \(B(M^*)\) is equivalent, up to the constant \(w^\top\mathbf1\), to minimizing \(w^\top x\) over \(B(M)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complementing every base reflects the base polytope through the all-ones vector and converts optimization on a matroid into opposite optimization on its dual.
knowledge_statements.title: Base-Polytope Duality

children.title: Integer Decomposition Property
children.top_down_role: Decomposition of integer points in dilated base polytopes into base incidence vectors.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[z=\chi^{B_1}+\cdots+\chi^{B_k}\quad\text{for some bases }B_1,\ldots,B_k\text{ of }M.\]

notation.meaning: k-fold dilation of the base polytope.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer decomposition property for finite matroid base polytopes.

source_refs.locator: 5.19 The integer rounding and decomposition properties p. 82
Section 6.3. Polyhedral Descriptions p. 144

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The base polytope \(B(M)\) has the integer decomposition property. Explicitly, for every positive integer \(k\) and every lattice point \(z\in kB(M)\cap\mathbb Z^E\), there exist bases \(B_1,\ldots,B_k\) of \(M\), with repetitions permitted, such that
\[z=\sum_{i=1}^k\chi^{B_i}.\]
Each coordinate \(z_e\) counts how many members of the resulting multiset of bases contain \(e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every lattice point in an integer dilation of a matroid base polytope is a sum of the same number of base-incidence vectors.
knowledge_statements.title: Integer Decomposition Property

source_witnesses.locator: 5.19 The integer rounding and decomposition properties p. 82

children.title: Duality-Compatible Decompositions
children.top_down_role: Behavior of integer decompositions under passage to dual base polytopes.

assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a finite matroid on \(E\), \(k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 1}\), and \(z\in kB(M)\cap\mathbb Z^E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\[k\mathbf1-z=\sum_{i=1}^k\chi^{E\setminus B_i}\in kB(M^*)\cap\mathbb Z^E,\]
\[\text{and complementation gives a bijection between the decompositions on the two sides.}\]

notation.meaning: Incidence vector of a base B.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility of base decompositions with matroid duality.

source_refs.locator: 5.19 The integer rounding and decomposition properties p. 82
Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the affine bijection \(z\mapsto k\mathbf1-z\) from \(kB(M)\) to \(kB(M^*)\), integer decompositions correspond term by term. If
\[z=\sum_{i=1}^k\chi^{B_i},\]
then every \(E\setminus B_i\) is a base of \(M^*\) and
\[k\mathbf1-z=\sum_{i=1}^k(\mathbf1-\chi^{B_i})=\sum_{i=1}^k\chi^{E\setminus B_i}.\]
Conversely, complementing the bases in any decomposition of \(k\mathbf1-z\) recovers a decomposition of \(z\). Thus the integer decomposition property and its decomposition fibers are preserved by matroid duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complementing every base converts any integer decomposition for a matroid base polytope bijectively into a decomposition for the dual base polytope.
knowledge_statements.title: Duality-Compatible Decompositions

children.title: Decomposition Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Nearby polyhedral settings where base-polytope decomposition behavior no longer transfers.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(1,1,1)\in2R_m\cap\mathbb Z^3\quad\text{but}\quad(1,1,1)\notin(R_m\cap\mathbb Z^3)+(R_m\cap\mathbb Z^3).\]

notation.meaning: Reeve lattice tetrahedron of height m.
Minkowski sum of sets A and B.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of integer decomposition after leaving the matroid-base-polytope class.

source_refs.locator: 5.19 The integer rounding and decomposition properties p. 82

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Integrality of a polytope alone does not imply integer decomposition. For \(m\ge2\), the Reeve tetrahedron
\[R_m:=\operatorname{conv}\{(0,0,0),(1,0,0),(0,1,0),(1,1,m)\}\]
is an integral polytope whose only lattice points are its four vertices. Nevertheless, \((1,1,1)\in2R_m\cap\mathbb Z^3\): using barycentric coefficients in the dilation, it is represented by coefficients \(1-1/m\), \(1-1/m\), and \(1/m\) on the three nonzero vertices, whose sum is at most \(2\). No sum of two vertices equals \((1,1,1)\). Thus removing the matroidal rank-submodular structure permits failure of integer decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integral polytopes need not have integer decomposition: a Reeve tetrahedron has a lattice point in its double that is not a sum of two lattice points.
knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition Failure Boundaries

source_witnesses.locator: 5.19 The integer rounding and decomposition properties p. 82

The statement also includes a barycentric verification and a nondecomposability argument, which are proof text. A direct source for the Reeve example is required before a clean proof-free replacement can be reviewed.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Order the elements with positive weight as \(e_1,\ldots,e_m\) so that \(w_{e_1}\geq\cdots\geq w_{e_m}>0\). Initialize \(I_0=\varnothing\). For \(j=1,\ldots,m\), set \(I_j=I_{j-1}\cup\{e_j\}\) when this set belongs to \(\mathcal I\), and otherwise set \(I_j=I_{j-1}\). Output \(I_g=I_m\). Then \(I_g\) maximizes \(w(I)\) over all \(I\in\mathcal I\), and its incidence vector maximizes \(w^\top x\) over \(P(M)\).

children.title: Rank-Inequality Separation
children.top_down_role: Separation interfaces for detecting violated rank constraints.

assumptions_latex: \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) is a finite matroid with rank function \(r\).
\(x\in\mathbb Q^E\) is the point to be separated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure returns \(S\subseteq E\) with \(x(S)>r(S)\), or certifies \(x(S)\leq r(S)\) for every \(S\subseteq E\).

notation.meaning: sum of coordinates indexed by a set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation concerns the exponential family of matroid rank inequalities only.

source_refs.locator: 5.1 Independence and rank p. 173

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Minimize the submodular function \(g_x(S)=r(S)-x(S)\) over \(S\subseteq E\). If a minimizer \(S^*\) satisfies \(g_x(S^*)<0\), return the violated valid inequality \(x(S^*)\leq r(S^*)\). If \(g_x(S^*)\geq0\), certify that every rank inequality \(x(S)\leq r(S)\) holds. Coordinate constraints such as \(x_e\geq0\) must be checked separately when separating over the full independence polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize rank minus coordinate sum. A negative minimum identifies a violated rank inequality; a nonnegative minimum certifies that all rank inequalities hold.
knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Inequality Separation

children.title: Most-Violated Rank Inequalities
children.top_down_role: Identification of rank constraints having maximum violation.

assumptions_latex: \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) is a finite matroid with rank function \(r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every minimizer of \(r(S)-x(S)\) indexes a rank inequality of maximum additive violation.

notation.meaning: additive violation of the rank inequality indexed by a set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive, rather than normalized, violation of matroid rank inequalities.

source_refs.locator: 5.1 Independence and rank p. 173

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(S\subseteq E\), define \(v_x(S)=x(S)-r(S)\). Then
\[\max_{S\subseteq E}v_x(S)=-\min_{S\subseteq E}\bigl(r(S)-x(S)\bigr).\]
Consequently, if \(S^*\in\arg\min_{S\subseteq E}(r(S)-x(S))\), then \(x(S^*)\leq r(S^*)\) is a most-additively-violated rank inequality. A rank inequality is violated exactly when the displayed maximum is positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A most-violated rank inequality is obtained by minimizing rank minus coordinate sum; the negative minimum equals the maximum additive violation.
knowledge_statements.title: Most-Violated Rank Inequalities

children.title: Separation-to-Violation Reductions
children.top_down_role: Structural relationships between ordinary separation and extremal violation queries.

assumptions_latex: A value oracle supplies \(r(S)\) for every \(S\subseteq E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Rank-inequality separation reduces to submodular minimization of \(g_x\) followed by a sign test.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle reduction from rank separation to submodular-function minimization.

source_refs.locator: Section 4.6. Separation and Optimization p. 93

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Form the value oracle \(g_x(S)=r(S)-x(S)\), which is submodular because \(r\) is submodular and \(x(S)\) is modular. Invoke a submodular-minimization algorithm to obtain \(S^*\in\arg\min_{S\subseteq E}g_x(S)\). If \(g_x(S^*)<0\), output \(x(S^*)\leq r(S^*)\); otherwise certify every rank inequality. Thus any polynomial-time submodular-minimization implementation yields polynomial-time rank-inequality separation under the rank-value oracle model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtract the modular coordinate sum from the submodular rank function, minimize the result, and use the minimum's sign to separate or certify feasibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Separation-to-Violation Reductions

knowledge_statements.title: Optimization–Separation Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong oracle equivalence for bounded well-described rational polyhedra in the Turing model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty bounded well-described rational polyhedron with a supplied facet-complexity bound \(\varphi\). There is an oracle-polynomial algorithm that, given a strong separation oracle for \(P\) and \(c\in\mathbb Q^n\), computes a maximizer of \(c^\top x\) over \(P\). Conversely, there is an oracle-polynomial algorithm that, given a strong optimization oracle for \(P\) and \(y\in\mathbb Q^n\), either certifies \(y\in P\) or returns \(a\in\mathbb Q^n\) satisfying \(a^\top y>\max_{x\in P}a^\top x\). The running times are polynomial in \(n\), \(\varphi\), and the binary encoding lengths of the rational query data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a bounded well-described rational polyhedron with a known facet-complexity bound, exact linear optimization and exact separation can each be implemented in oracle-polynomial time using an oracle for the other.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty bounded well-described rational polyhedron.
A valid facet-complexity bound \(\varphi\) for \(P\) is supplied.
Queries and objective vectors are rational.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong linear optimization over \(P\) and strong separation for \(P\) are oracle-polynomially equivalent, with complexity polynomial in \(n\), \(\varphi\), and the query encoding lengths.

children.title: Online Objective Regimes
children.top_down_role: Greedy limitations under sequential information or irrevocable choices.

assumptions_latex: Elements with arbitrary nonnegative weights arrive sequentially in adversarial order.
At most one element may be accepted, and acceptance is immediate and irrevocable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No deterministic online algorithm has a finite competitive ratio against the offline maximum without additional value or arrival assumptions.

notation.meaning: value obtained by an online algorithm on a sequence

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Present a first element of weight \(1\). If the algorithm rejects it, terminate; then \(\operatorname{ALG}=0\) and \(\operatorname{OPT}=1\). If the algorithm accepts it, present a second element of weight \(K\), where \(K>1\); rank-one feasibility forces rejection of the second element, so \(\operatorname{ALG}=1\) and \(\operatorname{OPT}=K\). Since \(K\) is arbitrary, no constant \(C<\infty\) guarantees \(\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma)\leq C\operatorname{ALG}(\sigma)\) for every arrival sequence \(\sigma\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under adversarial arrivals and irrevocable rank-one selection, accepting or rejecting the first item can both be exploited, precluding any finite deterministic competitive ratio.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Regime Greedy Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of the classical offline-linear matroid greedy theorem across objective and information regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Exact weight-ordered greedy for \(\max\{\sum_{e\in I}w_e:I\in\mathcal I\}\) relies jointly on linear additivity and complete offline knowledge. Removing additivity permits complementarity examples in which a locally best marginal choice blocks the optimum, even for a uniform matroid. Removing offline knowledge permits adversarial rank-one sequences for which every deterministic irrevocable rule has unbounded competitive ratio. Hence the exchange axiom alone supplies neither exact nonlinear marginal greedy nor bounded deterministic online greedy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matroid exchange guarantees classical greedy only in the offline linear regime; nonlinear complementarities and adversarial arrivals each independently destroy that guarantee.
assumptions_latex: Feasibility is a matroid independence family.
Greedy decisions use only currently visible weights or marginal gains and are irrevocable within the applicable regime.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The matroid exchange axiom does not extend exact greedy optimization from offline linear objectives to arbitrary nonlinear or adversarial online objectives.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: conclusion follows from the two explicit regime counterexamples

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Edmonds' Matroid Intersection Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Computes a maximum-cardinality set independent in two oracle-given matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given matroids $(E,\mathcal F_1)$ and $(E,\mathcal F_2)$ by independence oracles, initialize $X:=\varnothing$. For every $y\in E\setminus X$ and $i\in\{1,2\}$ compute $C_i(X,y):=\{x\in X\cup\{y\}:X\cup\{y\}\notin\mathcal F_i,\ (X\cup\{y\})\setminus\{x\}\in\mathcal F_i\}$. Construct $S_X,T_X$, and the exchange graph $G_X$. Find by BFS a shortest $S_X$-$T_X$ path $P$. If no such path exists, return $X$; otherwise set $X:=X\mathbin{\triangle}V(P)$ and repeat. The returned set belongs to $\mathcal F_1\cap\mathcal F_2$ and has maximum cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from the empty set, construct the two-matroid exchange graph, augment along a shortest source-to-target path found by breadth-first search, and stop when no augmenting path exists; the result is a maximum-cardinality common independent set.
assumptions_latex: (E,\mathcal F_1)\text{ and }(E,\mathcal F_2)\text{ are matroids on the same ground set}
\mathcal F_1\text{ and }\mathcal F_2\text{ are accessed by independence oracles}
S_X,T_X,G_X\text{ are the standard matroid-intersection exchange structures}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X\in\mathcal F_1\cap\mathcal F_2\quad\text{and}\quad |X|=\max\{|Y|:Y\in\mathcal F_1\cap\mathcal F_2\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ordered Multiple-Exchange Lemma
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives sufficient circuit-incidence conditions for simultaneous deletion and insertion to preserve independence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(E,\mathcal F)$ be a matroid, let $X\in\mathcal F$, and let $x_1,\ldots,x_s\in X$ and $y_1,\ldots,y_s\in E\setminus X$. If $x_k\in C(X,y_k)$ for every $k=1,\ldots,s$ and $x_j\notin C(X,y_k)$ whenever $1\leq j<k\leq s$, then $(X\setminus\{x_1,\ldots,x_s\})\cup\{y_1,\ldots,y_s\}\in\mathcal F$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If each inserted element has a designated removed element in its exchange circuit and no earlier removed element lies in a later exchange circuit, all designated exchanges can be performed simultaneously while preserving independence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left(X\setminus\{x_1,\ldots,x_s\}\right)\cup\{y_1,\ldots,y_s\}\in\mathcal F

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Intersection of Independence Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines intersections on a common ground set and records closure under finite intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given independence systems $(E,\mathcal F_1)$ and $(E,\mathcal F_2)$, their intersection is $(E,\mathcal F_1\cap\mathcal F_2)$. children.title: Maximum-Cardinality Common Independence
children.top_down_role: Common independent-set optimization under cardinality objectives.

assumptions_latex: \(M_1=(E,\mathcal I_1)\) and \(M_2=(E,\mathcal I_2)\) are finite matroids with rank functions \(r_1,r_2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max\{|I|:I\in\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2\}=\min_{U\subseteq E}\bigl(r_1(U)+r_2(E\setminus U)\bigr)\).

notation.meaning: rank functions of the two matroids

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Edmonds' cardinality matroid-intersection min–max theorem.

source_refs.locator: 3.2 An Efficient Cardinality Matroid-Intersection Algorithm and Consequences p. 89
source_refs.source_title: A First Course in Combinatorial Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every common independent set \(I\in\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2\) and every \(U\subseteq E\), one has \(|I|\leq r_1(U)+r_2(E\setminus U)\). Moreover, equality is attained after maximizing over common independent sets and minimizing over subsets:
\[\max_{I\in\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2}|I|=\min_{U\subseteq E}\left(r_1(U)+r_2(E\setminus U)\right).\]
Thus a common independent set and a subset attaining equal values form primal and dual optimality certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum size of a set independent in both matroids equals the minimum sum of complementary ranks, yielding matching primal and dual certificates.
knowledge_statements.title: Maximum-Cardinality Common Independence

children.title: Maximum-Weight Common Independence
children.top_down_role: Common independent-set optimization under element weights.

assumptions_latex: \(M_1=(E,\mathcal I_1)\) and \(M_2=(E,\mathcal I_2)\) are finite matroids accessible by independence oracles.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A maximum-weight common independent set can be computed in time polynomial in \(|E|\), \(L\), and the independence-oracle cost.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-polynomial weighted matroid intersection for rational linear weights.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 An Efficient Maximum-Weight Matroid-Intersection Algorithm p. 101
source_refs.source_title: A First Course in Combinatorial Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There exists an oracle-polynomial weighted matroid-intersection algorithm that returns a set
\[I^*\in\arg\max\left\{w(I):I\in\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2\right\}.\]
The algorithm uses independence-oracle queries to construct exchange graphs and performs weight-sensitive augmentations, with potentials or reduced costs maintaining optimality conditions. Its running time is polynomial in \(|E|\), the binary encoding length \(L\) of \(w\), and the cost of an independence-oracle call. Negative-weight elements need not occur in an optimal downward-closed solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted matroid intersection is solvable in oracle-polynomial time by exchange-graph augmentations with reduced-cost optimality conditions, despite the failure of simple weight-ordered greedy.
knowledge_statements.title: Maximum-Weight Common Independence

children.title: Cardinality-to-Weight Transition
children.top_down_role: Structural changes introduced when cardinality objectives acquire weights.

assumptions_latex: \(M_1=(E,\mathcal I_1)\) and \(M_2=(E,\mathcal I_2)\) are finite matroids.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The cardinality problem is the special case \(w(e)=1\) for every \(e\in E\), while the weighted problem optimizes \(w(I)=\sum_{e\in I}w(e)\).

notation.meaning: Family of sets independent in both matroids

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite weighted matroid intersection; cardinality is recovered by unit weights.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the common independent-set family \(\mathcal F=\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2\),
\[\max_{I\in\mathcal F}|I|=\max_{I\in\mathcal F}\sum_{e\in I}1.\]
Thus maximum-cardinality matroid intersection is exactly the unit-weight instance of
\[\max_{I\in\mathcal F}w(I),\qquad w(I)=\sum_{e\in I}w(e).\]
General weights may distinguish common independent sets having equal cardinality. If negative weights are allowed and neither cardinality nor a base constraint is imposed, an optimum need not have maximum cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximum cardinality is weighted matroid intersection with every element weight equal to one. General weights may distinguish sets of equal cardinality, and negative weights may favor smaller sets.
knowledge_statements.title: Cardinality-to-Weight Transition

children.title: Common-Base Feasibility
children.top_down_role: Existence questions for sets forming bases in both matroids.

assumptions_latex: \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are finite matroids on the same ground set \(E\).
Their rank functions are \(r_1\) and \(r_2\), and \(r_1(E)=r_2(E)=r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A common base exists exactly when \(r_1(X)+r_2(E\setminus X)\ge r\) for every \(X\subseteq E\).

notation.meaning: Rank function of the matroid indexed by i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equal-rank finite matroids on a common ground set.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A set \(B\subseteq E\) is a common base if \(B\in\mathcal B(M_1)\cap\mathcal B(M_2)\). Such a set exists if and only if
\[r_1(X)+r_2(E\setminus X)\ge r\qquad\text{for every }X\subseteq E.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two finite matroids of the same rank have a common base exactly when every subset of the ground set has complementary rank sum at least their common rank.

children.title: Common-Base Optimization
children.top_down_role: Objective-driven selection among feasible common bases.

assumptions_latex: \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are finite matroids on \(E\) with common rank \(r\).
At least one common base exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The problem is to find \(B^*\in\mathcal B(M_1)\cap\mathcal B(M_2)\) satisfying \(w(B^*)=\max_B w(B)\).

notation.meaning: Set of bases of a matroid

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum-weight common bases of two equal-rank finite matroids.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 An Efficient Maximum-Weight Matroid-Intersection Algorithm p. 101
source_refs.source_title: A First Course in Combinatorial Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The maximum-weight common-base problem is
\[\max\left\{w(B):B\in\mathcal B(M_1)\cap\mathcal B(M_2)\right\},\qquad w(B)=\sum_{e\in B}w(e).\]
An output \(B^*\) is optimal when \(B^*\) is a base of each matroid and \(w(B^*)\ge w(B)\) for every common base \(B\). Because every feasible set has cardinality \(r\), adding the same constant to all element weights does not change the set of optimal common bases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Among all sets that are bases of both matroids, choose one with maximum additive element weight. Uniform weight shifts preserve the optimizers.
knowledge_statements.title: Common-Base Optimization

children.title: Common-Base Infeasibility Certificates
children.top_down_role: Structural witnesses for failure of common-base feasibility.

assumptions_latex: \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are finite matroids on \(E\) with rank functions \(r_1\) and \(r_2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any \(X\subseteq E\) with \(r_1(X)+r_2(E\setminus X)<r\) certifies that no common base exists.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A subset \(X\subseteq E\) is a common-base infeasibility certificate if
\[r_1(X)+r_2(E\setminus X)<r.\]
The certificate is verifiable using rank evaluations for \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) and establishes that \(\mathcal B(M_1)\cap\mathcal B(M_2)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subset whose rank in the first matroid plus the rank of its complement in the second is below the common rank is a verifiable certificate that no common base exists.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Matroid intersection satisfies
\[\max\left\{|I|:I\in\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2\right\}=\min_{X\subseteq E}\left(r_1(X)+r_2(E\setminus X)\right).\]
Accordingly, a common independent set \(I^*\) and a subset \(X^*\subseteq E\) form a rank-partition optimality certificate when
\[|I^*|=r_1(X^*)+r_2(E\setminus X^*).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A common independent set and a ground-set partition certify maximum cardinality when the set's size equals the complementary rank sum of that partition.

children.title: Common-Base Duality
children.top_down_role: Dual structures governing common-base feasibility and optimization.

assumptions_latex: \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are finite matroids on \(E\) with equal rank \(r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A common base \(B\) exists exactly when \(E\) partitions as \(B\dot\cup(E\setminus B)\) into bases of \(M_1\) and \(M_2^*\).

notation.meaning: Dual matroid of the second matroid

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common bases expressed through matroid duality and complementary bases.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(B\subseteq E\),
\[B\in\mathcal B(M_2)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad E\setminus B\in\mathcal B(M_2^*).\]
Consequently,
\[B\in\mathcal B(M_1)\cap\mathcal B(M_2)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad B\in\mathcal B(M_1)\ \text{ and }\ E\setminus B\in\mathcal B(M_2^*).\]
Thus common-base feasibility is equivalent to partitioning \(E\) into a base of \(M_1\) and a base of \(M_2^*\). Under equal ranks, this complementary-base formulation is equivalent to the rank-partition inequalities for common-base feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is a common base precisely when it is a base of the first matroid and its complement is a base of the second matroid's dual.
knowledge_statements.title: Common-Base Duality

children.title: Menger-Type Matroid Duality
children.top_down_role: Connectivity-style dual interpretations within matroid intersection.

assumptions_latex: \(M_U\) and \(M_V\) are the partition matroids on \(F\) allowing at most one edge incident with each vertex of their respective sides.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Matroid intersection specializes to \(\nu(G)=\tau(G)\), the bipartite matching-cover min-max equality.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bipartite matching as the Menger-type separation specialization of matroid intersection.

source_refs.locator: 4.3 Duality and a Maximum-Cardinality Matching Algorithm p. 113

source_refs.locator: 3.2 An Efficient Cardinality Matroid-Intersection Algorithm and Consequences p. 89
source_refs.source_title: A First Course in Combinatorial Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A subset of \(F\) is independent in both \(M_U\) and \(M_V\) exactly when it is a matching of \(G\). Under this specialization, the matroid-intersection rank-partition formula yields the bipartite matching min-max relation
\[\nu(G)=\tau(G),\]
where \(\nu(G)\) is the maximum number of pairwise vertex-disjoint edges and \(\tau(G)\) is the minimum number of vertices meeting every edge. This is Menger-type duality: a maximum packing of disjoint objects equals a minimum separating or covering obstruction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the two endpoint partition matroids of a bipartite graph, common independent sets are matchings, and matroid-intersection duality becomes maximum matching equals minimum vertex cover.
knowledge_statements.title: Menger-Type Matroid Duality

children.title: Directed Exchange Graphs
children.top_down_role: Directed representations of feasible exchanges between matroid elements.

assumptions_latex: \(M_1=(E,\mathcal I_1)\) and \(M_2=(E,\mathcal I_2)\) are finite matroids.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The directed exchange graph records all one-element exchanges preserving independence in either matroid and all admissible augmentation endpoints.

notation.meaning: Directed exchange graph relative to I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard directed exchange graph for cardinality matroid intersection.

source_refs.locator: 3.2 An Efficient Cardinality Matroid-Intersection Algorithm and Consequences p. 89

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The directed exchange graph \(D_I\) has vertex set \(E\). For \(x\in I\) and \(y\in E\setminus I\), include the arc \(y\to x\) when \(I-x+y\in\mathcal I_1\), and include the arc \(x\to y\) when \(I-x+y\in\mathcal I_2\). Define
\[S_I=\{y\in E\setminus I:I+y\in\mathcal I_1\},\qquad T_I=\{y\in E\setminus I:I+y\in\mathcal I_2\}.\]
Directed paths from \(S_I\) to \(T_I\) encode alternating sequences of exchanges between the two matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The directed exchange graph orients feasible first-matroid exchanges toward the current set and feasible second-matroid exchanges away from it, with addable elements as sources and sinks.
knowledge_statements.title: Directed Exchange Graphs

children.title: Border Graphs
children.top_down_role: Boundary-oriented graph representations used in intersection methods.

assumptions_latex: \(M_1,M_2\) and the common independent set \(I\) are finite.
The term border graph is interpreted as the colored bipartite exchange encoding underlying \(D_I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The border graph records the same elementary exchanges as \(D_I\), with edge color retaining the responsible matroid.

notation.meaning: Colored bipartite border graph relative to I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Provisional colored bipartite interpretation; the local meaning of “border graph” requires source confirmation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The border graph \(H_I\) is the bipartite multigraph with vertex classes \(I\) and \(E\setminus I\). For \(x\in I\) and \(y\in E\setminus I\), place a color-
\(1\) edge between \(x\) and \(y\) when \(I-x+y\in\mathcal I_1\), and place a color-
\(2\) edge when \(I-x+y\in\mathcal I_2\). If both conditions hold, retain both colors. Mark each \(y\in S_I\) as an entry border and each \(y\in T_I\) as an exit border.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Provisionally, a border graph is the colored bipartite encoding of feasible exchanges between a common independent set and its complement, with entry and exit elements marked.
knowledge_statements.title: Border Graphs

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weighted Matroid Intersection Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-dual augmenting-sequence method for maximum-weight common independent sets given independence oracles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given matroids $(E,\mathcal F_1)$ and $(E,\mathcal F_2)$ through independence oracles and weights $c:E\to\mathbb R$, initialize $X_0=\varnothing$, $c_1=c$, and $c_2=0$. At each iteration construct the two directed exchange-arc sets from the fundamental circuits $C_i(X_k,y)$, the source and target sets $S,T$, and the tight subgraph defined by equal $c_i$-values. If a tight $\bar S$--$\bar T$ path $P$ exists, choose one having the minimum number of edges and set $X_{k+1}=X_k\triangle V(P)$. Otherwise, for the set $R$ reachable from $\bar S$, compute $\varepsilon=\min\{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2,\varepsilon_3,\varepsilon_4\}$ from the exchange-arc and source/target slacks, using $\min\varnothing=\infty$. If $\varepsilon<\infty$, replace $c_1(x)$ by $c_1(x)-\varepsilon$ and $c_2(x)$ by $c_2(x)+\varepsilon$ for every $x\in R$ and continue; if $\varepsilon=\infty$, return a maximum-weight member of $\{X_0,\ldots,X_k\}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from the empty common independent set, repeatedly build the two-matroid exchange digraph using fundamental circuits and the current split weights. Augment along a shortest tight source-to-target path when one exists. Otherwise adjust the split weights by the minimum exchange or endpoint slack, with the minimum of an empty set interpreted as infinity. When no finite adjustment remains, return the heaviest common independent set encountered.
assumptions_latex: $(E,\mathcal F_1)$ and $(E,\mathcal F_2)$ are matroids on the same finite ground set $E$, supplied by independence oracles.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}\{c(Z):Z\in\mathcal F_1\cap\mathcal F_2\}.

knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Polynomial Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong polynomiality in the independence-oracle model for exact weighted matroid intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the independence-oracle model, a regime is strongly polynomial when there exist polynomials \(Q\) and \(A\) such that every instance on \(n\) elements is solved using at most \(Q(n)\) oracle calls and \(A(n)\) other arithmetic operations, irrespective of the numerical values and binary encoding lengths of the weights. Additionally, every number produced during the computation must have encoding length bounded polynomially in the total input encoding length. A bound polynomial in \(\log\max_{e\in E}|w(e)|\) alone establishes ordinary polynomiality, not strong polynomiality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong polynomiality requires operation and oracle-call bounds depending only on ground-set size, not on weight magnitudes, together with intermediate encodings bounded polynomially in the total input encoding length.
assumptions_latex: Inputs are two finite matroids on \(E\), accessed through a specified independence oracle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A weighted-intersection algorithm is strongly polynomial only if its oracle-call count and its remaining arithmetic-operation count are bounded by a polynomial in \(|E|\), independently of the numerical weight magnitudes, and every intermediate number has encoding length bounded polynomially in the total input encoding length.

The common independent-set polytope is
\[P=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^E_{\ge 0}:x(S)\le r_1(S)\text{ and }x(S)\le r_2(S)\text{ for every }S\subseteq E\right\}.\]
Equivalently, \(P=P(M_1)\cap P(M_2)\), where \(P(M_i)\) is the independent-set polytope of \(M_i\). The matroid-intersection polyhedral theorem states that this intersection is integral and therefore
\[P=\operatorname{conv}\left\{\chi^I:I\in\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The intersection of two matroid independent-set polytopes is integral and is exactly the convex hull of incidence vectors of sets independent in both matroids.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The common-base polytope is the rank-\(r\) face of the common independent-set polytope:
\[B(M_1,M_2)=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^E_{\ge0}:x(E)=r,\ x(S)\le r_i(S)\text{ for every }S\subseteq E\text{ and }i\in\{1,2\}\right\}.\]
Because the common independent-set polytope is integral, this face is integral. Its integral points are precisely the incidence vectors \(\chi^B\) of sets \(B\subseteq E\) having size \(r\) and independent in both matroids, equivalently bases of both matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For equal-rank matroids, imposing total coordinate sum equal to the common rank yields exactly the convex hull of their common bases.

children.title: Common-Base Convex Hull
children.top_down_role: Convex-hull viewpoint for common-base families.

knowledge_statements.title: Common-Base Convex Hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incidence-vector hull for common bases of two finite matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M_1=(E,\mathcal I_1)\) and \(M_2=(E,\mathcal I_2)\) be finite matroids, and suppose their common-base family \(\mathcal B_{12}=\{B\subseteq E:B\text{ is a base of both }M_1\text{ and }M_2\}\) is nonempty. The common-base convex hull is
\[
P_{\mathrm{CB}}(M_1,M_2)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^B:B\in\mathcal B_{12}\}\subseteq\mathbb R^E,
\]
where \(\chi^B_e=1\) exactly when \(e\in B\). Equivalently, it is the smallest convex subset of \(\mathbb R^E\) containing every common-base incidence vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The common-base hull is the convex hull of the incidence vectors of all sets that are bases of both matroids.
assumptions_latex: \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are finite matroids on the same ground set \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{\mathrm{CB}}(M_1,M_2)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^B:B\in\mathcal B_{12}\}\).

children.title: Common-Base Hull Operations
children.top_down_role: Optimization, separation, projection, and related operations on the common-base hull.

knowledge_statements.title: Common-Base Hull Operations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exposed faces and linear optimization over the common-base hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(P=P_{\mathrm{CB}}(M_1,M_2)\) and \(w\in\mathbb R^E\), define the exposed maximizing face by \(F_w(P)=\{x\in P:w^\top x=h_P(w)\}\), where \(h_P(w)=\max_{x\in P}w^\top x\). Then
\[
h_P(w)=\max_{B\in\mathcal B_{12}}\sum_{e\in B}w_e,
\qquad
F_w(P)=\operatorname{conv}\left\{\chi^B:B\in\mathcal B_{12},\ \sum_{e\in B}w_e=h_P(w)\right\}.
\]
Thus linear optimization and exposed-face extraction commute with passing from common bases to their convex hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimizing a linear weight over the hull is equivalent to optimizing over common bases; the optimal incidence vectors generate the exposed face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_w(P)\) is the convex hull of the maximum-weight common-base incidence vectors.

children.title: Intersection Facet Structure

knowledge_statements.title: Intersection Facet Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank-inequality description of the common-independent-set polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M_i=(E,\mathcal I_i)\) have rank function \(r_i\) for \(i\in\{1,2\}\). The common-independent-set polytope satisfies
\[
P_{12}=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^I:I\in\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2\}
=\{x\in\mathbb R^E:x_e\geq0\ (e\in E),\ x(S)\leq r_i(S)\ (S\subseteq E,\ i=1,2)\}.
\]
Consequently, after restricting to the affine hull and deleting redundant inequalities, every facet is supported by a nonnegativity equality or by a tight rank equality \(x(S)=r_i(S)\). The displayed system does not assert that every listed inequality defines a facet.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Common independent sets have a rank-inequality hull; its facets arise from irredundant nonnegativity or rank inequalities, although many listed inequalities may be redundant.
assumptions_latex: \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are finite matroids on the same ground set \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{12}=\{x\geq0:x(S)\leq r_i(S)\text{ for all }S\subseteq E,\ i=1,2\}\).

children.title: Intersection Polytope Integrality
children.top_down_role: Integral structure of common independent-set polyhedra.

knowledge_statements.title: Intersection Polytope Integrality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite two-matroid common-independent-set integrality theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M_1=(E,\mathcal I_1)\) and \(M_2=(E,\mathcal I_2)\) be finite matroids with rank functions \(r_1,r_2\). Then the polyhedron
\[
Q=\{x\in\mathbb R^E:x_e\geq0\ (e\in E),\ x(S)\leq r_1(S),\ x(S)\leq r_2(S)\ (S\subseteq E)\}
\]
is integral, and
\[
Q=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^I:I\in\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2\}.
\]
In particular, every vertex of \(Q\) is a zero-one incidence vector of a set independent in both matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The intersection of two matroid independence polytopes is integral, with vertices precisely among incidence vectors of common independent sets.
assumptions_latex: \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are finite matroids on a common ground set \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^I:I\in\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2\}\), so \(Q\) is integral.

notation.meaning: intersection of the two rank-inequality polyhedra

children.title: Facet-Based Integrality Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Relationships between defining facets and integral polyhedral structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Facet-Based Integrality Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer facet data alone do not guarantee polyhedral integrality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An integral right-hand side in a facet description is insufficient for integrality. Indeed, consider
\[
P=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:x_i\geq0\ (i=1,2,3),\ x_1+x_2\leq1,\ x_1+x_3\leq1,\ x_2+x_3\leq1\}.
\]
All coefficients and right-hand sides are integral, but \((1/2,1/2,1/2)\) is a vertex of \(P\). Therefore the integrality of the matroid-intersection rank system requires additional structure, such as the two-matroid intersection theorem; it cannot be inferred merely by inspecting integer-valued facet normals and bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integer facet coefficients and bounds do not imply integral vertices; the fractional stable-set relaxation of a triangle supplies a concrete counterexample.
assumptions_latex: The polyhedron is interpreted over \(\mathbb R^3\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((1/2,1/2,1/2)\in\operatorname{vert}(P)\), so \(P\) is not integral.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The triangle relaxation is a mathematically appropriate failure boundary, and the three tight pair inequalities certify that the displayed fractional point is a vertex. However, the record contains no citation or explicit standard-field rationale, so it does not satisfy the evidence contract for this nontrivial counterexample and interface claim.

children.title: Matching Applications
children.top_down_role: Encodings of matching problems through matroid intersection.

knowledge_statements.title: Matching Applications
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bipartite matching as intersection of two partition matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(U,V;E)\) be a finite bipartite graph. On ground set \(E\), let \(M_U\) be the partition matroid imposing \(|F\cap\delta(u)|\leq1\) for every \(u\in U\), and let \(M_V\) impose \(|F\cap\delta(v)|\leq1\) for every \(v\in V\). Then
\[
F\text{ is a matching in }G
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
F\in\mathcal I(M_U)\cap\mathcal I(M_V).
\]
Hence maximum-cardinality and maximum-weight bipartite matching are instances of, respectively, cardinality and weighted matroid intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bipartite matching is exactly a common independent set of the two partition matroids enforcing one selected edge at each endpoint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal M(G)=\mathcal I(M_U)\cap\mathcal I(M_V)\).

children.title: Rainbow Selection Applications

knowledge_statements.title: Rainbow Selection Applications
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rainbow independent selection as matroid intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite matroid, and let \(E=C_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}C_k\) be a coloring partition. Let \(M_C\) be the partition matroid with capacities one on the color classes. Then
\[
X\in\mathcal I\cap\mathcal I(M_C)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
X\text{ is independent in }M\text{ and }|X\cap C_j|\leq1\text{ for every }j.
\]
Thus maximum-cardinality or maximum-weight rainbow independent selection is a matroid-intersection problem. A full rainbow transversal exists exactly when the maximum common-independent-set cardinality is \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Intersecting a matroid with the color partition matroid produces exactly its rainbow independent sets; size k certifies one representative from every color.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal I\cap\mathcal I(M_C)\) is the family of rainbow sets independent in \(M\).

notation.meaning: color partition matroid with unit capacities

children.title: Representative-System Applications

knowledge_statements.title: Representative-System Applications
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Systems of distinct representatives encoded by two partition matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite family \((A_i)_{i\in I}\) of subsets of a finite set \(U\), define \(E=\{(i,u):i\in I,\ u\in A_i\}\). Let \(M_I\) partition \(E\) by the first coordinate with capacity one, and let \(M_U\) partition it by the second coordinate with capacity one. A set \(F\subseteq E\) is common independent exactly when it is a partial system of distinct representatives. Moreover,
\[
|F|=|I|
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
F=\{(i,f(i)):i\in I\}
\]
for a system of distinct representatives \(f(i)\in A_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choosing distinct representatives is equivalent to finding a common independent set of two partition matroids that has one pair for every indexed set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A system of distinct representatives exists if and only if \(M_I\) and \(M_U\) have a common independent set of size \(|I|\).

notation.meaning: the index and representative partition matroids

children.title: Matching-to-Selection Reductions

knowledge_statements.title: Matching-to-Selection Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction of bipartite matching to common independent-set selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a finite bipartite graph \(G=(U,V;E)\) with edge weights \(w:E\to\mathbb R\). Construct the endpoint partition matroids \(M_U,M_V\) on \(E\), each with unit capacity on the incident-edge blocks. Run a cardinality or weighted matroid-intersection algorithm on \((M_U,M_V)\), using the independence tests
\[
F\in\mathcal I(M_U)\Longleftrightarrow |F\cap\delta(u)|\leq1\quad(u\in U),
\]
and analogously for \(V\). Stop when the intersection algorithm certifies optimality and output its common independent set \(F\); this \(F\) is an optimal matching for the same objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Build one unit-capacity partition matroid for each side of a bipartite graph, then solve their intersection to obtain an optimal matching.
assumptions_latex: Edge weights are explicitly available when weighted matching is requested.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The common-independent-set output is a maximum-cardinality or maximum-weight matching in \(G\).

children.title: Branching Applications
children.top_down_role: Directed branching problems represented through matroid intersection.

knowledge_statements.title: Branching Applications
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed branchings encoded as graphic and partition-matroid intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph. Let \(M_G\) be the graphic matroid on \(A\) obtained by forgetting arc orientations, and let \(M_{\mathrm{in}}\) be the partition matroid whose blocks are arcs entering each vertex, with capacity one. Then
\[
B\in\mathcal I(M_G)\cap\mathcal I(M_{\mathrm{in}})
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
(V,B)\text{ is a branching forest},
\]
meaning that its underlying undirected graph is acyclic and every vertex has indegree at most one. Consequently, maximum-weight branching forests are weighted matroid-intersection instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed branching forest is exactly a common independent set of the underlying graphic matroid and the unit indegree partition matroid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal B(D)=\mathcal I(M_G)\cap\mathcal I(M_{\mathrm{in}})\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The graphic-matroid and indegree-partition-matroid characterization is standard under the stated definition of a branching forest, and representation is the correct content kind. Nevertheless, the record supplies neither a source nor an explicit standard-field rationale; a branching reference is also needed to anchor the chosen terminology.

children.title: Matroidal Linkage Applications
children.top_down_role: Linkage problems subject to matroidal selection constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Matroidal Linkage Applications
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vertex-disjoint directed linkage defines a strict gammoid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph and \(T\subseteq V\). Call \(X\subseteq V\) linkable to \(T\) if there exist \(|X|\) pairwise vertex-disjoint directed paths whose initial vertices are precisely \(X\) and whose terminal vertices are distinct members of \(T\), allowing a length-zero path when its vertex lies in \(T\). Then
\[
\mathcal I(D,T)=\{X\subseteq V:X\text{ is linkable to }T\}
\]
is the independent-set family of a matroid on \(V\), called the strict gammoid presented by \((D,T)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The vertex sets that can be linked by disjoint directed paths to distinct terminals form the independent sets of a strict gammoid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((V,\mathcal I(D,T))\) is a matroid.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

children.title: Branching-to-Linkage Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Structural connections between branching and matroidal linkage formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Branching-to-Linkage Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Path extraction connecting branching forests with vertex-disjoint linkages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\) be a branching forest in a finite digraph, and let \(R\) contain the unique indegree-zero root of each nontrivial component. If \(T\) contains at most one vertex from each weak component of \((V,B)\), then the unique directed root-to-\(t\) paths for \(t\in T\) are pairwise vertex-disjoint and form a linkage from a subset of \(R\) to \(T\). Conversely, any family of pairwise vertex-disjoint directed paths has an arc union that is a branching forest. Thus path extraction and path union provide the basic branching-to-linkage interface under the one-terminal-per-component condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Selecting at most one terminal per branching component yields disjoint root-to-terminal paths; conversely, a vertex-disjoint path family has a branching arc union.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) meets each weak component of \((V,B)\) at most once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected root-to-terminal paths form a vertex-disjoint linkage, and every vertex-disjoint directed path family has branching arc union.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No supporting citation or standard-field rationale is supplied, and the formulation has a boundary-case gap: R is required to contain roots only of nontrivial components, while T may contain a vertex from an isolated component, so the asserted linkage from a subset of R need not exist. A source-backed version must either include the roots of all components and allow length-zero paths or restrict T to nontrivial components.

children.title: Two-Matroid Tractability
children.top_down_role: Algorithmic tractability specific to intersection of two matroids.

knowledge_statements.title: Two-Matroid Tractability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-model tractability of weighted intersection for two finite matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M_1=(E,\mathcal I_1)\) and \(M_2=(E,\mathcal I_2)\) be finite matroids, let \(w:E\to\mathbb Q\), and suppose independence in each matroid is available through an oracle. A maximum-weight common independent set can be computed using a number of arithmetic operations and oracle calls polynomial in \(|E|\) and the binary encoding length of \(w\). In particular, the unweighted problem \(\max\{|I|:I\in\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2\}\) is polynomial-time solvable in the independence-oracle model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximum-weight intersection of two finite matroids is polynomial-time solvable when each matroid is accessed through an independence oracle.
assumptions_latex: \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are finite matroids on the same ground set \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max\{w(I):I\in\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2\}\) is computable in oracle-polynomial time.

children.title: Multi-Matroid Hardness

knowledge_statements.title: Multi-Matroid Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hardness begins with three input matroids when their number is not fixed at two.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given three finite matroids \(M_i=(E,\mathcal I_i)\) and an integer \(q\), deciding whether there exists \(I\subseteq E\) such that \(I\in\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2\cap\mathcal I_3\) and \(|I|\ge q\) is NP-complete, even when all three matroids are partition matroids presented explicitly. Membership in NP follows by checking the three capacity systems. Hardness follows from the equivalent formulation of three-dimensional matching: triples are ground elements, and each coordinate induces one partition matroid requiring distinct coordinate values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finding a common independent set of prescribed size becomes NP-complete for three matroids, already for explicitly represented partition matroids.
assumptions_latex: The three partition matroids and \(q\) are explicitly encoded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists I\subseteq E:\ |I|\ge q\ \text{and}\ I\in\bigcap_{i=1}^3\mathcal I_i\) is NP-complete to decide.

notation.meaning: Independent sets of the ith partition matroid.

children.title: Constraint-Count Complexity Boundary

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Count Complexity Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity dichotomy between two-way and three-way matroid intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite matroids given by independence oracles, maximizing a linear weight over the common independent sets of two matroids is polynomial-time solvable. No analogous polynomial-time guarantee holds merely from fixing one additional matroid: the cardinality decision problem for the intersection of three explicitly represented partition matroids is NP-complete. Thus the passage from two to three matroid constraints is a sharp worst-case complexity boundary, unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two-matroid intersection is polynomial-time solvable, whereas three-matroid intersection is NP-complete even for partition matroids.
assumptions_latex: Finite ground sets and standard independence-oracle or explicit partition-matroid encodings are used.
Complexity is measured in the ordinary deterministic Turing model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Two constraints admit polynomial-time optimization, while three constraints admit no general polynomial-time algorithm unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\).

notation.meaning: Class of polynomially verifiable decision problems.

children.title: Matroid Union Theorem Family
children.top_down_role: Union and partition are kept together with their rank certificates, augmenting algorithms, capacitated variants, and base packing and covering consequences.

knowledge_statements.title: Matroid Union Theorem Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite matroid-union theorem in rank and independence forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M_i=(E,\mathcal I_i)\), \(i=1,\ldots,k\), be finite matroids with rank functions \(r_i\). The family \(\mathcal I=\{I_1\cup\cdots\cup I_k:I_i\in\mathcal I_i\}\) is the independent-set family of a matroid \(M_1\vee\cdots\vee M_k\). Its rank function satisfies
\[
r_{\vee}(X)=\min_{T\subseteq X}\left(|X\setminus T|+\sum_{i=1}^k r_i(T)\right)\qquad(X\subseteq E).
\]
Consequently, \(X\subseteq E\) belongs to \(\mathcal I\) exactly when \(|A|\le\sum_{i=1}^k r_i(A)\) for every \(A\subseteq X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unions of independent sets form a matroid whose rank has a min-formula; subset rank inequalities exactly characterize union independence.
assumptions_latex: \(M_1,\ldots,M_k\) are finite matroids on a common ground set \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal I\) is matroidal and \(r_{\vee}(X)=\min_{T\subseteq X}(|X\setminus T|+\sum_i r_i(T))\).

notation.meaning: Rank function of the union matroid.
Rank function of input matroid i.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Partitionable Sets and Matroid Union
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the union, also called the sum, of finitely many matroids on the same ground set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(E,\mathcal F_1),\ldots,(E,\mathcal F_k)$ be matroids. A set $X\subseteq E$ is partitionable if there is a partition $X=X_1\cup\cdots\cup X_k$ such that $X_i\in\mathcal F_i$ for every $i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}$. If $\mathcal F$ is the family of all partitionable subsets of $E$, then $(E,\mathcal F)$ is called the union or sum of these matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For matroids on a common ground set, a subset is partitionable when it can be partitioned into sets independently feasible in the respective matroids. The family of all such subsets defines their union, or sum.
assumptions_latex: (E,\mathcal F_i)\text{ is a matroid for each }i=1,\ldots,k
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal F=\{X\subseteq E:\exists\text{ a partition }X=X_1\cup\cdots\cup X_k\text{ with }X_i\in\mathcal F_i\ \forall i\},\quad (E,\mathcal F)\text{ is the union (sum).}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matroid Union Theorem and Rank Formula
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure under matroid union and the associated rank min-formula for matroids on a common ground set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $(E,\mathcal F_1),\ldots,(E,\mathcal F_k)$ be matroids with rank functions $r_1,\ldots,r_k$, and let $(E,\mathcal F)$ be their union. Then $(E,\mathcal F)$ is a matroid, and for every $X\subseteq E$,
\[
r(X)=\min_{A\subseteq X}\left(|X\setminus A|+\sum_{i=1}^k r_i(A)\right).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The union of matroids on a common ground set is itself a matroid. For every subset X, its union-matroid rank is the minimum over subsets A of X of the number of elements in X outside A plus the sum of the component ranks of A.
assumptions_latex: (E,\mathcal F_i)\text{ is a matroid with rank function }r_i\text{ for each }i=1,\ldots,k
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (E,\mathcal F)\text{ is a matroid, and }\forall X\subseteq E,\quad r(X)=\min_{A\subseteq X}\left(|X\setminus A|+\sum_{i=1}^k r_i(A)\right).

children.title: Union Rank Evaluation

knowledge_statements.title: Union Rank Evaluation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimization representation for evaluating the rank of a matroid union.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For finite matroids \(M_i=(E,\mathcal I_i)\) with rank functions \(r_i\), the rank of their union on any \(X\subseteq E\) is
\[
r_{\vee}(X)=\min_{T\subseteq X}\left(|X|-|T|+\sum_{i=1}^k r_i(T)\right).
\]
Equivalently, evaluating \(r_{\vee}(X)\) reduces to minimizing the integer-valued submodular function \(T\mapsto |X|-|T|+\sum_i r_i(T)\) over subsets of \(X\). Any minimizing set \(T\) certifies the returned rank value by attaining the displayed minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Union rank equals the minimum of a rank-sum plus the number of elements excluded from a chosen subset.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_{\vee}(X)=\min_{T\subseteq X}(|X|-|T|+\sum_i r_i(T))\).

notation.meaning: Subset used in the rank minimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Union Feasibility Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subset certificates for feasible and infeasible matroid-union decompositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M_i=(E,\mathcal I_i)\), \(i=1,\ldots,k\), be finite matroids with rank functions \(r_i\), and let \(X\subseteq E\). Exactly one of the following alternatives holds: (i) there are sets \(I_i\in\mathcal I_i\) such that \(X=I_1\cup\cdots\cup I_k\), which may be chosen pairwise disjoint; or (ii) there is a set \(A\subseteq X\) such that \(|A|>\sum_{i=1}^k r_i(A)\). The data in (i) certify feasibility, while the set in (ii) certifies infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid independent-set decomposition certifies feasibility; otherwise, a subset whose size exceeds the sum of its ranks certifies infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Either \(X=\bigcup_i I_i\) with \(I_i\in\mathcal I_i\), or \(\exists A\subseteq X:\ |A|>\sum_i r_i(A)\), but not both.

notation.meaning: Independent part assigned to matroid i.

children.title: Rank-Based Feasibility Tests
children.top_down_role: Use of union-rank structure to distinguish feasible from infeasible instances.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Based Feasibility Tests
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient rank inequalities for covering a prescribed set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M_i=(E,\mathcal I_i)\), \(i=1,\ldots,k\), be finite matroids with rank functions \(r_i\). For a prescribed set \(X\subseteq E\), there exist sets \(I_i\in\mathcal I_i\) satisfying \(X=I_1\cup\cdots\cup I_k\) if and only if
\[
|A|\le \sum_{i=1}^k r_i(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\subseteq X.
\]
It is sufficient to test subsets of \(X\); elements outside \(X\) play no role in the feasibility predicate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is decomposable among the matroids exactly when every one of its subsets has size at most the corresponding rank sum.
assumptions_latex: \(M_1,\ldots,M_k\) are finite matroids on the same ground set \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X\in\mathcal I(M_1\vee\cdots\vee M_k)\iff \forall A\subseteq X,\ |A|\le\sum_i r_i(A)\).

notation.meaning: Rank of A in matroid i.

knowledge_statements.title: Matroid-Union Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independence polytope of the finite matroid union.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M=M_1\vee\cdots\vee M_k\) be the union matroid on finite ground set \(E\), with union rank function \(r_{\vee}\). Its independence polytope is
\[
P(M)=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^E_{\ge0}:x(A)\le r_{\vee}(A)\text{ for every }A\subseteq E\right\}.
\]
Using the union-rank formula, the right-hand sides may equivalently be written as \(r_{\vee}(A)=\min_{T\subseteq A}(|A\setminus T|+\sum_i r_i(T))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The matroid-union polyhedron is the nonnegative rank-inequality polytope determined by the union matroid's rank function.
assumptions_latex: \(r_{\vee}\) is the rank function of their union.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P(M)=\{x\in\mathbb R^E_{\ge0}:x(A)\le r_{\vee}(A)\ \forall A\subseteq E\}\).

notation.meaning: The sum of coordinates indexed by A.

children.title: Union Polytope Integrality
children.top_down_role: Integral structure of polyhedra arising from matroid union.

knowledge_statements.title: Union Polytope Integrality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integrality of the finite matroid-union independence polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For finite matroids \(M_1,\ldots,M_k\) on \(E\), let \(M=M_1\vee\cdots\vee M_k\). The polytope
\[
P(M)=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^E_{\ge0}:x(A)\le r_{\vee}(A)\text{ for all }A\subseteq E\right\}
\]
is integral: every vertex belongs to \(\{0,1\}^E\). Moreover, its integral points are exactly the incidence vectors of independent sets of the union matroid, equivalently of sets expressible as unions \(I_1\cup\cdots\cup I_k\) with \(I_i\in\mathcal I_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every vertex of the union independence polytope is integral and represents a set decomposable into independent sets of the input matroids.
assumptions_latex: \(M_1,\ldots,M_k\) are finite matroids on the same ground set \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{vert}(P(M))\subseteq\{0,1\}^E\), and \(P(M)\cap\mathbb Z^E=\{\chi^I:I\in\mathcal I(M)\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Integral Hull Descriptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-hull description for incidence vectors of union-independent sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M=M_1\vee\cdots\vee M_k\) be a finite matroid union with rank function \(r_{\vee}\). Then
\[
\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^I:I\in\mathcal I(M)\}
=
\left\{x\in\mathbb R^E:x\ge0,\ x(A)\le r_{\vee}(A)\text{ for every }A\subseteq E\right\}.
\]
Equivalently, substituting the union-rank formula gives the valid right-hand side \(x(A)\le\min_{T\subseteq A}(|A\setminus T|+\sum_i r_i(T))\) for every \(A\subseteq E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rank inequalities give the exact convex hull of incidence vectors of sets decomposable among the input matroids.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^I:I\in\mathcal I(M)\}=\{x\ge0:x(A)\le r_{\vee}(A)\ \forall A\subseteq E\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Augmenting Union Algorithms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exchange-path augmentation for maximum-cardinality matroid union.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input finite matroids \(M_i=(E,\mathcal I_i)\) through independence oracles. Initialize pairwise disjoint \(I_i=\varnothing\). For an uncovered element, construct the exchange graph whose labeled move \(e\to f\) in class \(i\) is allowed when \((I_i\setminus\{f\})\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I_i\); a path terminates when its current element can be inserted into some class without displacement. Apply the exchanges backward to increase \(|\bigcup_i I_i|\) by one. Repeat until no augmenting path exists, then output \(\bigcup_i I_i\), which has maximum cardinality in \(M_1\vee\cdots\vee M_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly route an uncovered element through valid exchanges; each augmenting path increases the covered set, and absence of one proves optimality.
assumptions_latex: Each \(M_i\) is a finite matroid on \(E\) with an independence oracle.
The maintained sets \(I_i\) are pairwise disjoint and independent in their respective matroids.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output \(I=\bigcup_i I_i\) satisfies \(|I|=r_{\vee}(E)\).

notation.meaning: Current elements assigned to matroid i.

knowledge_statements.title: Matroid Partition Algorithms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructive feasibility algorithm for partitioning a ground set among matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input finite matroids \(M_i=(E,\mathcal I_i)\) through independence oracles and initialize \(I_i=\varnothing\). Process elements by attempting to insert each uncovered \(e\) into a class; if direct insertion fails, search the labeled exchange graph for a sequence of displacements ending at a class admitting insertion. Apply such a sequence and continue. If every element is assigned, output the partition \(E=I_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}I_k\). If augmentation fails, output a reachable-set obstruction \(A\subseteq E\) satisfying \(|A|>\sum_i r_i(A)\), which certifies that no feasible partition exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exchange-path augmentation either partitions all elements into appropriate independent sets or returns a subset violating the rank-sum condition.
assumptions_latex: \(M_1,\ldots,M_k\) are finite matroids on \(E\) with independence oracles.
Each maintained part \(I_i\) is independent in \(M_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm returns either \(E=\mathbin{\dot\bigcup}_i I_i\) with \(I_i\in\mathcal I_i\), or \(A\subseteq E\) with \(|A|>\sum_i r_i(A)\).

children.title: Weighted Matroid-Union Variants
children.top_down_role: Matroid-union problems with element-weight objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Matroid-Union Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common element-weight version of finite matroid union.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M_i=(E,\mathcal I_i)\), for \(i=1,\ldots,k\), be matroids with rank functions \(r_i\), and let \(w:E\to\mathbb R\). A set \(I\subseteq E\) is union-independent exactly when it can be partitioned as \(I=I_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}I_k\) with \(I_i\in\mathcal I_i\). Consequently, the weighted matroid-union problem has the representation
\[\max\left\{\sum_{e\in E}w(e)x_e:x\in\{0,1\}^{E},\ \sum_{e\in F}x_e\leq\sum_{i=1}^{k}r_i(F)\ \text{for every }F\subseteq E\right\}.\]
An optimal support is a maximum-weight independent set of the union matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted matroid union maximizes element weight over sets partitionable into one independent set from each constituent matroid, equivalently over the displayed rank-inequality system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{supp}(x)\in\mathcal I_1\vee\cdots\vee\mathcal I_k\), and the displayed maximum is the weighted union optimum.

notation.meaning: Rank function of the matroid M_i.
Independent-set family of the union matroid.

children.title: Capacitated Matroid-Union Variants
children.top_down_role: Matroid-union problems with multiplicity or capacity restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Capacitated Matroid-Union Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Assignment-capacity extension allowing an element in several constituent independent sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M_i=(E,\mathcal I_i)\), for \(i=1,\ldots,k\), be matroids, and let \(b\in\mathbb Z_+^E\). A capacitated union assignment is a tuple \((I_1,\ldots,I_k)\) satisfying
\[I_i\in\mathcal I_i\quad(i=1,\ldots,k),\qquad \left|\{i:e\in I_i\}\right|\leq b_e\quad(e\in E).\]
Equivalently, its binary incidence vectors satisfy \(y^i\in\{0,1\}^E\), \(\operatorname{supp}(y^i)\in\mathcal I_i\), and \(\sum_{i=1}^k y^i_e\leq b_e\) for every \(e\in E\). The usual disjoint matroid union is recovered when \(b_e=1\) for every \(e\in E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A capacitated union assignment selects one independent set per matroid while limiting how many selected sets may use each ground element.
assumptions_latex: \(b_e\) is a nonnegative integer for every \(e\in E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((I_1,\ldots,I_k)\) is feasible exactly when all constituent-independence and element-load constraints hold.

notation.meaning: Maximum permitted number of constituent sets using element e.
Indicator that element e is assigned to the i-th independent set.

children.title: Weighted Capacitated Union

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Capacitated Union
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Assignment-weighted optimization over capacitated matroid-union selections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For matroids \(M_i=(E,\mathcal I_i)\), capacities \(b\in\mathbb Z_+^E\), and assignment weights \(w_{i,e}\in\mathbb R\), weighted capacitated union is
\[\max\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{e\in E}w_{i,e}y^i_e:\ y^i\in\{0,1\}^{E},\ \operatorname{supp}(y^i)\in\mathcal I_i,\ \sum_{i=1}^{k}y^i_e\leq b_e\ \text{for every }e\in E\right\}.\]
The formulation permits different rewards for assigning the same element to different matroids. With \(b_e=1\) and \(w_{i,e}=w_e\), it specializes to common-weight matroid union.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted capacitated union chooses independent assignments of maximum total reward subject to a usage capacity for every element.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed integer program is the weighted capacitated-union optimum.

notation.meaning: Reward for assigning element e to matroid i.

children.title: Fractional Base Packing

knowledge_statements.title: Fractional Base Packing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacity-weighted fractional packing in the base hypergraph of a matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) have base family \(\mathcal B\), and let \(c\in\mathbb R_+^E\) be element capacities. A fractional base packing is a vector \(\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^{\mathcal B}\) satisfying
\[\sum_{B\in\mathcal B:e\in B}\lambda_B\leq c_e\qquad(e\in E).\]
Its value is \(\sum_{B\in\mathcal B}\lambda_B\), and the fractional base-packing number is
\[\nu_f(M,c)=\max\left\{\sum_{B\in\mathcal B}\lambda_B:\lambda\geq0,\ \sum_{B\ni e}\lambda_B\leq c_e\ \text{for every }e\in E\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fractional base packing assigns nonnegative weights to bases so that the total weight using each element does not exceed its capacity.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a finite matroid with at least one base.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nu_f(M,c)\) is the maximum total feasible base weight.

notation.meaning: Fractional multiplicity assigned to base B.

knowledge_statements.title: Fractional Base Covering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Demand-weighted fractional covering by matroid bases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) have base family \(\mathcal B\), and let \(d\in\mathbb R_+^E\) be element demands. A fractional base covering is a vector \(\mu\in\mathbb R_+^{\mathcal B}\) satisfying
\[\sum_{B\in\mathcal B:e\in B}\mu_B\geq d_e\qquad(e\in E).\]
Its cost under unit base costs is \(\sum_{B\in\mathcal B}\mu_B\), and the fractional covering number is
\[\tau_f(M,d)=\min\left\{\sum_{B\in\mathcal B}\mu_B:\mu\geq0,\ \sum_{B\ni e}\mu_B\geq d_e\ \text{for every }e\in E\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fractional base covering weights bases so that their total weight through every element meets that element's demand.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\tau_f(M,d)\) is the minimum total base weight satisfying all demands.

notation.meaning: Fractional multiplicity assigned to base B.

children.title: Fractional Packing–Covering Duality
children.top_down_role: Dual relationship between fractional base packing and covering parameters.

knowledge_statements.title: Fractional Packing–Covering Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: LP duality for capacity packing and demand covering over the base-incidence matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite matroid with base family \(\mathcal B\), linear-programming duality gives
\[\nu_f(M,c)=\min\left\{\sum_{e\in E}c_e y_e:y\in\mathbb R_+^E,\ \sum_{e\in B}y_e\geq1\ \text{for every }B\in\mathcal B\right\},\]
and
\[\tau_f(M,d)=\max\left\{\sum_{e\in E}d_e z_e:z\in\mathbb R_+^E,\ \sum_{e\in B}z_e\leq1\ \text{for every }B\in\mathcal B\right\}.\]
Thus fractional base packing is dual to an element cover of all bases, while fractional base covering is dual to an element packing constrained on every base.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: LP duality converts base weights into element prices: packing yields base-covering inequalities, while covering yields base-packing inequalities.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is finite and has at least one base.
\(c,d\in\mathbb R_+^E\), and the relevant primal optimum is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The two displayed primal-dual optimum equalities hold.

notation.meaning: Dual price for packing capacity at element e.

children.title: Integer Base Packing

knowledge_statements.title: Integer Base Packing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Edmonds' finite base-packing criterion and min-max formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite matroid of positive rank \(r(E)\). There exist \(k\) pairwise disjoint bases if and only if
\[|E\setminus X|\geq k\bigl(r(E)-r(X)\bigr)\qquad\text{for every }X\subseteq E.\]
Consequently, the maximum number of pairwise disjoint bases is
\[\nu(M)=\min_{\substack{X\subseteq E\\r(X)<r(E)}}\left\lfloor\frac{|E\setminus X|}{r(E)-r(X)}\right\rfloor.\]
The minimum is taken only over subsets with positive denominator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matroid contains k disjoint bases exactly when every subset leaves enough outside elements to supply k copies of its rank deficit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nu(M)=\min_{X:r(X)<r(E)}\left\lfloor |E\setminus X|/(r(E)-r(X))\right\rfloor\).

notation.meaning: Maximum number of pairwise disjoint bases.

children.title: Integer Base Covering

knowledge_statements.title: Integer Base Covering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite matroid-union criterion for covering the ground set by bases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite loopless matroid with rank function \(r\), and let \(k\) be a positive integer. The ground set \(E\) can be covered by \(k\) bases, with overlaps allowed, if and only if
\[|X|\leq k\,r(X)\qquad\text{for every }X\subseteq E.\]
Consequently, the minimum number of bases covering \(E\) is
\[\tau(M)=\max_{\varnothing\neq X\subseteq E}\left\lceil\frac{|X|}{r(X)}\right\rceil.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite loopless matroid can be covered by k bases exactly when every subset has cardinality at most k times its rank; hence its minimum base-covering number is the displayed maximum of rounded-up cardinality-to-rank ratios.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\tau(M)=\max_{\varnothing\neq X\subseteq E}\left\lceil |X|/r(X)\right\rceil\).

notation.meaning: Minimum number of bases whose union is E.

children.title: Integer Packing–Covering Gap
children.top_down_role: Structural differences between integral packing and covering parameters.

knowledge_statements.title: Integer Packing–Covering Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbounded separation between integer base-packing and base-covering numbers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each integer \(m\geq1\), let \(M_m\) be the partition matroid on two nonempty blocks \(P_1,P_2\) with \(|P_1|=1\), \(|P_2|=m\), and capacity one on each block. Every base contains one element from each block. Therefore any two bases intersect in the unique element of \(P_1\), so \(\nu(M_m)=1\). Covering every element of \(P_2\) requires at least \(m\) bases and is achievable with \(m\) bases, so \(\tau(M_m)=m\). Thus \(\tau(M_m)-\nu(M_m)=m-1\), showing that no universal additive packing-covering bound exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A two-block partition matroid with block sizes one and m has packing number one and covering number m, producing an unbounded additive gap.
assumptions_latex: Each base of \(M_m\) selects exactly one element from each block.
