children.title: Blocking-Polyhedron View
children.top_down_role: Blocking geometry associated with base-covering structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Blocking-Polyhedron View
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Upward-closed polyhedral representation of covering constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A blocking polyhedron is a nonempty polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb R_+^E\) satisfying \(P+\mathbb R_+^E=P\). For a finite nonempty family \(\mathcal S\subseteq2^E\), its incidence-vector dominant
\[P_{\mathcal S}=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^S:S\in\mathcal S\}+\mathbb R_+^E\]
is a blocking polyhedron. Its blocker is
\[b(P_{\mathcal S})=\{y\in\mathbb R_+^E:\langle y,x\rangle\geq1\ \text{for every }x\in P_{\mathcal S}\}=\{y\in\mathbb R_+^E:y(S)\geq1\ \text{for every }S\in\mathcal S\}.\]
Thus the nonnegative vectors covering every member of \(\mathcal S\) are precisely the members of \(b(P_{\mathcal S})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A blocking polyhedron is a nonempty upward-closed nonnegative polyhedron. The blocker of a set-family incidence dominant consists exactly of the nonnegative vectors assigning weight at least one to every represented set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b(P_{\mathcal S})=\{y\in\mathbb R_+^E:y(S)\geq1\text{ for every }S\in\mathcal S\}\).

notation.meaning: Dominant of the incidence vectors of the set family.

children.title: Antiblocking-Polyhedron View
children.top_down_role: Antiblocking geometry associated with base-packing structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Antiblocking-Polyhedron View
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Downward-closed convex representation of packing constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A convex corner is a nonempty compact convex set \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R_+^E\) that is lower-comprehensive: if \(x\in Q\) and \(0\leq x'\leq x\), then \(x'\in Q\). Its antiblocker is
\[\operatorname{abl}(Q)=\{y\in\mathbb R_+^E:\langle y,x\rangle\leq1\ \text{for every }x\in Q\}.\]
The set \(\operatorname{abl}(Q)\) is again a convex corner. If \(D\subseteq\mathbb R_+^E\) is finite and \(Q=\operatorname{conv}(D)\) is a convex corner, then
\[\operatorname{abl}(Q)=\{y\in\mathbb R_+^E:\langle y,d\rangle\leq1\ \text{for every }d\in D\},\]
which is a packing-inequality representation indexed by \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Antiblocking maps a compact downward-closed nonnegative convex set to the nonnegative vectors whose scalar product with every feasible vector is at most one; for a finite generating set, it suffices to impose the inequalities on the generators.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) is a convex corner in \(\mathbb R_+^E\).
When a generating set is used, \(D\subseteq\mathbb R_+^E\) is finite and \(Q=\operatorname{conv}(D)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{abl}(Q)\) is a convex corner, with the displayed finite inequality description when \(Q=\operatorname{conv}(D)\).

notation.meaning: Antiblocker of the convex corner Q.
Finite generating set whose convex hull is Q.

children.title: Blocking–Antiblocking Polarity
children.top_down_role: Polar relationship connecting the two geometric viewpoints.

knowledge_statements.title: Blocking–Antiblocking Polarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Involutive polarity for nonnegative blocking polyhedra and convex corners.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R_+^E\) be a nonempty closed convex blocking polyhedron with \(0\notin P\), and let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R_+^E\) be a convex corner. Define
\[b(P)=\{y\geq0:\langle y,x\rangle\geq1\ \text{for every }x\in P\},\qquad \operatorname{abl}(Q)=\{y\geq0:\langle y,x\rangle\leq1\ \text{for every }x\in Q\}.\]
Nonnegative separation yields the involutions
\[b(b(P))=P,\qquad \operatorname{abl}(\operatorname{abl}(Q))=Q.\]
Accordingly, either member of a blocking or antiblocking polar pair determines the other uniquely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Taking the blocker twice recovers a closed blocking polyhedron, and taking the antiblocker twice recovers a convex corner.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is nonempty, closed, convex, blocking, and excludes the origin.
\(Q\) is nonempty, compact, convex, and lower-comprehensive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b(b(P))=P\) and \(\operatorname{abl}(\operatorname{abl}(Q))=Q\).

notation.meaning: Blocking polar defined by scalar products at least one.
Antiblocking polar defined by scalar products at most one.

children.title: Graph Arboricity
children.top_down_role: Arboricity viewed through graphic-matroid union.

knowledge_statements.title: Graph Arboricity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines arboricity for finite loopless multigraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite loopless multigraph \(G=(V,E)\), its arboricity is
\[
a(G):=\min\bigl\{k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}:E=F_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}F_k,\ (V,F_i)\text{ is a forest for every }i\bigr\}.
\]
The empty graph has \(a(G)=0\). Parallel edges are permitted, but no forest may contain two parallel edges joining the same vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The arboricity of a finite loopless multigraph is the minimum number of forests whose edge sets partition all its edges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a(G)\) is the minimum size of a partition of \(E\) into forests.

children.title: Forest Partition
children.top_down_role: Partition of edge sets into forests through matroid-union structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Forest Partition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a fixed-size forest partition of a graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite loopless multigraph and let \(k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\). A \(k\)-forest partition of \(G\) is an ordered family \((F_1,\ldots,F_k)\) of pairwise disjoint subsets of \(E\) such that
\[
E=\bigcup_{i=1}^{k}F_i
\quad\text{and}\quad
(V,F_i)\text{ is acyclic for every }i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}.
\]
Empty parts are allowed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A k-forest partition assigns every edge to one of k parts so that each part induces an acyclic spanning subgraph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((F_1,\ldots,F_k)\) partitions \(E\) and every \((V,F_i)\) is a forest.

notation.meaning: the edge set of forest part i

children.title: Arboricity–Partition Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural correspondence between arboricity bounds and forest partitions.

knowledge_statements.title: Arboricity–Partition Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nash-Williams arboricity formula in graphic-matroid form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite loopless multigraph. For nonempty \(F\subseteq E\), let \(V(F)\) be the vertices incident with \(F\), and let \(c(F)\) be the number of connected components of \((V(F),F)\). Then \(E\) can be partitioned into \(k\) forests if and only if
\[
|F|\le k\bigl(|V(F)|-c(F)\bigr)
\quad\text{for every nonempty }F\subseteq E.
\]
Consequently,
\[
a(G)=\max_{\varnothing\ne F\subseteq E}\left\lceil\frac{|F|}{|V(F)|-c(F)}\right\rceil,
\]
with \(a(G)=0\) when \(E=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph decomposes into k forests exactly when every edge subset has size at most k times its graphic rank; the maximum density ceiling equals arboricity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E\) is partitionable into \(k\) forests exactly under the displayed subset inequalities, and their least feasible \(k\) equals \(a(G)\).

notation.meaning: vertices incident with edges in F
number of components of the edge-induced subgraph on V(F)

children.title: Matroid Coloring
children.top_down_role: Partition-based coloring of a matroid ground set.

knowledge_statements.title: Matroid Coloring
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the chromatic number of a finite matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite matroid. A proper \(k\)-coloring is a map \(\varphi:E\to\{1,
\ldots,k\}\) such that every color class \(\varphi^{-1}(i)\) belongs to \(\mathcal I\). The matroid chromatic number is
\[
\chi(M):=\min\bigl\{k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}:E\text{ is the union of }k\text{ independent sets}\bigr\}.
\]
Set \(\chi(M)=\infty\) if \(M\) has a loop, and \(\chi(M)=0\) if \(E=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The chromatic number of a finite matroid is the minimum number of independent color classes covering its ground set; a loop makes it infinite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\chi(M)\) is the least number of independent sets whose union is \(E\).

notation.meaning: family of independent sets of M

children.title: Matroid List Coloring
children.top_down_role: Matroid coloring under element-specific color availability.

knowledge_statements.title: Matroid List Coloring
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines list colorability and list chromatic number for finite matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite matroid. Given finite color lists \(L(e)\) for \(e\in E\), an \(L\)-coloring is a map \(\varphi:E\to\bigcup_{e\in E}L(e)\) such that \(\varphi(e)\in L(e)\) for every \(e\), and each color class \(\varphi^{-1}(c)\) is independent. The list chromatic number \(\chi_\ell(M)\) is the least \(k\) such that an \(L\)-coloring exists whenever \(|L(e)|\ge k\) for all \(e\). It is \(\infty\) when \(M\) has a loop.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The list chromatic number is the least k guaranteeing an independent-class coloring from every assignment of at least k allowed colors per element.
assumptions_latex: Each \(L(e)\) is a finite set of colors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\chi_\ell(M)\) is the universal list-size threshold for a proper matroid coloring.

children.title: Coloring-to-List-Coloring Transfer
children.top_down_role: Structural relationships between ordinary and list-constrained matroid coloring.

knowledge_statements.title: Coloring-to-List-Coloring Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Seymour's list-coloring theorem for finite matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every finite matroid \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\),
\[
\chi_\ell(M)=\chi(M).
\]
Equivalently, if \(E\) can be partitioned into \(k\) independent sets and every element \(e\in E\) is assigned a list \(L(e)\) with \(|L(e)|\ge k\), then there exists a choice \(\varphi(e)\in L(e)\) such that every color class \(\varphi^{-1}(c)\) is independent. The equality uses the convention that both parameters are \(\infty\) when \(M\) has a loop.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite matroid has equal ordinary and list chromatic numbers: any feasible k-coloring transfers to every assignment of lists having at least k colors per element.
assumptions_latex: \(k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\), and \(|L(e)|\ge k\) for every \(e\in E\) in the equivalent formulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\chi_\ell(M)=\chi(M)\).

children.title: Matroid Density Parameters
children.top_down_role: Rank-normalized density measures relevant to union applications.

knowledge_statements.title: Matroid Density Parameters
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines maximum rank density for a finite matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M=(E,r)\) be a finite matroid. Its maximum rank density is
\[
\gamma(M):=\max_{\varnothing\ne A\subseteq E}\frac{|A|}{r(A)},
\]
where a quotient with \(r(A)=0\) is interpreted as \(\infty\). Thus \(\gamma(M)=\infty\) exactly when \(M\) has a loop. For \(E=\varnothing\), set \(\gamma(M)=0\). The integral density parameter is \(d(M):=\lceil\gamma(M)\rceil\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximum matroid density is the largest ratio of a nonempty subset's size to its rank; its ceiling is the integral density parameter.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma(M)=\max_{\varnothing\ne A\subseteq E}|A|/r(A)\) and \(d(M)=\lceil\gamma(M)\rceil\).

children.title: Matroid Covering Parameters

knowledge_statements.title: Matroid Covering Parameters
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines independent-set covering and partition parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite matroid \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\), define
\[
\kappa(M):=\min\bigl\{k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}:E=I_1\cup\cdots\cup I_k,\ I_i\in\mathcal I\text{ for every }i\bigr\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(\kappa(M)\) is the minimum number of independent sets whose pairwise-disjoint union is \(E\). Set \(\kappa(M)=\infty\) if \(M\) has a loop and \(\kappa(M)=0\) when \(E=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The covering parameter is the least number of independent sets covering the ground set, equivalently the least number of independent sets partitioning it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa(M)\) is both the minimum independent-cover size and the minimum independent-partition size.

notation.meaning: an independent member of the cover

children.title: Density–Covering Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural links between density thresholds and covering requirements.

knowledge_statements.title: Density–Covering Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matroid-union characterization of independent-set covering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M=(E,r)\) be a finite matroid and let \(k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\). The ground set \(E\) can be covered, equivalently partitioned, by \(k\) independent sets if and only if
\[
|A|\le k\,r(A)
\quad\text{for every }A\subseteq E.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\kappa(M)=\max_{\varnothing\ne A\subseteq E}\left\lceil\frac{|A|}{r(A)}\right\rceil
=\lceil\gamma(M)\rceil,
\]
with the conventions \(\kappa(M)=\gamma(M)=\infty\) when \(M\) has a loop and both equal \(0\) when \(E=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matroid is coverable by k independent sets exactly when every subset has size at most k times its rank; the covering number is ceiling density.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E\) is coverable by \(k\) independent sets iff \(|A|\le kr(A)\) for all \(A\subseteq E\), and \(\kappa(M)=\lceil\gamma(M)\rceil\).

source_witnesses.locator: 5.5 Matroid algorithms and polyhedra p. 192

knowledge_statements.title: Matroidal Systems of Representatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rado's independent-transversal theorem for finite set families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M=(E,r)\) be a finite matroid and let \((A_i)_{i\in I}\) be a finite family of subsets of \(E\). There exist pairwise distinct representatives \(x_i\in A_i\) for all \(i\in I\) such that \(\{x_i:i\in I\}\) is independent in \(M\) if and only if
\[
r\left(\bigcup_{i\in J}A_i\right)\ge |J|
\quad\text{for every }J\subseteq I.
\]
Such a choice is called a matroidal, or independent, system of representatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A family has distinct representatives independent in a matroid exactly when every subfamily's union has rank at least the subfamily's size.
assumptions_latex: \((A_i)_{i\in I}\) is a finite family of subsets of \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An independent system of distinct representatives exists iff \(r(\bigcup_{i\in J}A_i)\ge |J|\) for every \(J\subseteq I\).

children.title: Transversal Rank
children.top_down_role: Rank structure arising from transversal selection systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Transversal Rank
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rado's min-max formula for maximum partial independent transversals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M=(E,r)\) be a finite matroid and let \((A_i)_{i\in I}\) be a finite family of subsets of \(E\). Let \(\nu_M(A)\) be the largest cardinality of a set \(K\subseteq I\) for which there are pairwise distinct elements \(x_i\in A_i\), indexed by \(i\in K\), with \(\{x_i:i\in K\}\) independent in \(M\). Then
\[
\nu_M(A)=\min_{J\subseteq I}\left(|I\setminus J|+r\left(\bigcup_{i\in J}A_i\right)\right).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum size of a partial independent transversal equals a minimum combining omitted indices with the rank of a selected subfamily's union.
assumptions_latex: \((A_i)_{i\in I}\) is a finite family of subsets of \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nu_M(A)=\min_{J\subseteq I}(|I\setminus J|+r(\bigcup_{i\in J}A_i))\).

notation.meaning: subfamily index set in the min-max formula

children.title: Transversal Deficiency Certificates
children.top_down_role: Witnesses measuring failure of full transversal selection.

knowledge_statements.title: Transversal Deficiency Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank-deficient subfamilies certify missing independent representatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite matroid \(M=(E,r)\) and family \((A_i)_{i\in I}\), define the deficiency of \(J\subseteq I\) by
\[
\delta(J):=|J|-r\left(\bigcup_{i\in J}A_i\right).
\]
If \(\delta(J)=d>0\), then every partial independent transversal omits at least \(d\) indices, so \(J\) is a verifiable deficiency certificate. Moreover, if \(\nu_M(A)\) is the maximum partial independent-transversal size, then
\[
|I|-\nu_M(A)=\max_{J\subseteq I}\delta(J).
\]
Thus a maximizing \(J\) certifies the exact optimum deficit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subfamily whose size exceeds the rank of its union certifies unavoidable omissions; maximum such deficiency equals the exact transversal deficit.
assumptions_latex: \((A_i)_{i\in I}\) is a finite family of subsets of \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \(J\subseteq I\) certifies deficit \(\delta(J)\), and \(|I|-\nu_M(A)=\max_{J\subseteq I}\delta(J)\).

A parity solution is a subfamily \(P\subseteq\Pi\) for which the union of its pairs is independent, namely
\[\bigcup_{p\in P}p\in\mathcal I.\]

\[\nu(M,\Pi)=\max\left\{|P|:P\subseteq\Pi,\ \bigcup_{p\in P}p\in\mathcal I\right\}.\]

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A fractional matroid-matching cover is a finite family \((z_X)_{X\subseteq V}\) satisfying \(z_X\geq0\) and
\[\sum_{X\subseteq V}|e\cap X|z_X\geq1\qquad(e\in E_G).\]
Its cost is \(c(z)=\sum_{X\subseteq V}r_M(X)z_X\). For every matroid matching \(F\), independence of \(V(F)\) gives \(|V(F)\cap X|\leq r_M(X)\); consequently the displayed edge-cover conditions certify
\[|F|\leq c(z).\]

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite linear-programming duality applied to matroid rank inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: LP matching-covering duality; integral equality requires exactness of the rank relaxation.

source_refs.locator: Linear Programming and Duality p. 14

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(\nu_f(G,M)\) by maximizing \(\sum_{e\in E_G}x_e\) subject to \(x_e\geq0\) and
\[\sum_{e\in E_G}|e\cap X|x_e\leq r_M(X)\qquad(X\subseteq V).\]
Its linear-programming dual is the minimum-cost fractional cover of the preceding record, so
\[\nu(G,M)\leq\nu_f(G,M)=\tau_f(G,M).\]
Moreover, \(\nu(G,M)=\tau_f(G,M)\) holds exactly when the relaxation admits an optimal incidence vector of a matroid matching. Thus strong fractional duality is unconditional, while integral matching-covering equality is an additional structural property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The rank-constrained fractional matching program and fractional cover program are LP duals; an integral min-max equality holds precisely when the relaxation is exact.
knowledge_statements.title: Matching–Covering Duality

source_witnesses.locator: Linear Programming and Duality p. 14

assumptions_latex: \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) is finite and \(\Pi\) partitions \(E\) into pairs.
A search routine is complete for the specified class of augmenting sequences.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Repeated feasible augmentation terminates, and completeness makes the terminal parity family maximum.

notation.meaning: Symmetric difference of two pair families.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract augmentation framework; concrete admissible sequences depend on the represented matroid class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input \((M,\Pi)\), initialize \(P=\varnothing\), and repeatedly search for an ordered family \(Q=(q_1,\ldots,q_t)\) of distinct pairs such that
\[P'=P\mathbin{\triangle}\{q_1,\ldots,q_t\},\qquad |P'|=|P|+1,\qquad \bigcup_{p\in P'}p\in\mathcal I.\]
When such an augmenting sequence is found, replace \(P\) by \(P'\). Stop when the class-specific completeness criterion certifies that no augmenting sequence exists, and output \(P\). Cardinality increases at every update, so termination occurs after at most \(|\Pi|\) augmentations; correctness requires the cited completeness property for the chosen sequence system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from no pairs, repeatedly toggle an admissible alternating sequence that increases the feasible family by one; a complete sequence system certifies optimality at termination.
knowledge_statements.title: Augmenting-Sequence Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record does not specify an admissible augmenting-sequence system or a search procedure. It defines augmentation as finding any larger feasible solution and assumes a class-specific completeness criterion, so it is not a substantive algorithm for the terminal container.

assumptions_latex: \(M\) is represented over a field \(\mathbb F\) of characteristic different from \(2\).
Each pair \(p_i\) is represented by columns \(a_i,b_i\in\mathbb F^r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\nu(M,\Pi)=\frac12\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb F(y_1,\ldots,y_m)}\left(\sum_{i=1}^m y_i(a_ib_i^{\mathsf T}-b_ia_i^{\mathsf T})\right).\]

notation.meaning: Algebraically independent indeterminates, one per pair.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical symbolic skew-matrix formulation of linear matroid parity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear matroid parity over fields of characteristic other than two.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p_i=\{a_i,b_i\}\) for \(1\leq i\leq m\), and introduce algebraically independent indeterminates \(y_1,\ldots,y_m\). Form the skew-symmetric symbolic matrix
\[A(y)=\sum_{i=1}^m y_i\bigl(a_ib_i^{\mathsf T}-b_ia_i^{\mathsf T}\bigr).\]
Then its rank over the rational-function field records the optimum parity size:
\[\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb F(y_1,\ldots,y_m)}A(y)=2\nu(M,\Pi).\]
Consequently, symbolic elimination, randomized specialization over sufficiently large fields, or exact polynomial-identity methods can determine the linear matroid-parity value through matrix rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a linear matroid, twice the maximum number of feasible pairs equals the generic rank of a symbolic skew-symmetric matrix built from the pair columns.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Algebraic Matroid-Parity Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The symbolic skew-matrix rank correspondence is a specialized theorem central to the record and requires an authoritative source with an exact theorem or section locator.

children.title: Combinatorial Methods for Special Matroid Classes

assumptions_latex: A matroid class supplies an independence oracle and a complete, terminating combinatorial augmentation routine for parity instances in that class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The routine returns a maximum-cardinality parity family after at most \(|\Pi|\) successful augmentations.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: oracle-level specialization of augmenting-sequence methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle template for classes admitting complete combinatorial augmentation; no universal complexity bound is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \((M,\Pi)\), set \(P=\varnothing\). Invoke the class-specific combinatorial search routine on \(P\). If it returns a feasible augmentation \(P'\subseteq\Pi\) with
\[|P'|=|P|+1\quad\text{and}\quad\bigcup_{p\in P'}p\in\mathcal I,\]
replace \(P\) by \(P'\) and repeat. If it returns its prescribed no-augmentation certificate, output \(P\). Under the assumed completeness property, the certificate implies that no larger feasible parity family exists. Since every successful iteration increases \(|P|\), at most \(|\Pi|\) successful augmentations occur; the total running time is determined by the class-specific search routine.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a special matroid class with complete combinatorial augmentation, repeatedly enlarge the feasible pair family; the class-specific no-augmentation certificate establishes optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Combinatorial Methods for Special Matroid Classes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record assumes the complete class-specific routine that the leaf is supposed to describe. It names no special matroid class, augmentation rule, or implementable combinatorial method, so it does not fill the exact container.

assumptions_latex: \(A(y)\) is the symbolic skew-symmetric matrix of a linear matroid-parity instance over \(K=\mathbb F(y_1,\ldots,y_m)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\nu(M,\Pi)=\min\{k:A(y)=PQ,\ P\in K^{r\times 2k},\ Q\in K^{2k\times r}\}.\]

notation.meaning: Rational-function field of the symbolic matrix.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: generic-rank characterization combined with rank factorization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic min-max form for represented linear matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The generic-rank characterization and rank-factorization theorem give
\[2\nu(M,\Pi)=\operatorname{rank}_{K}A(y)=\min\{s:A(y)=PQ,\ P\in K^{r\times s},\ Q\in K^{s\times r}\}.\]
Because a skew-symmetric matrix over \(K\) has even rank, this is equivalently
\[\nu(M,\Pi)=\min\{k:A(y)=PQ,\ P\in K^{r\times 2k},\ Q\in K^{2k\times r}\}.\]
Thus the maximum number of independent prescribed pairs equals the minimum half-dimension of an exact factorization of the associated symbolic matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the linear regime, the maximum parity size equals the minimum half-width of an exact factorization of the symbolic skew matrix.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Regime Min–Max Structure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The factorization equality follows from the claimed generic-rank correspondence and ordinary rank factorization, but the specialized matroid-parity correspondence has no supporting source.

children.title: Linear-Regime Covering Certificates
children.top_down_role: Covering witnesses available under linear representation.

assumptions_latex: \(A(y)\in K^{r\times r}\) is the symbolic parity matrix over \(K=\mathbb F(y_1,\ldots,y_m)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An identity \(A(y)=PQ\) with inner dimension \(2k\) certifies \(\nu(M,\Pi)\leq k\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: matrix rank factorization supplies an algebraic upper certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic upper certificates over the rational-function field of a linear parity representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A linear-regime covering certificate of value \(k\) is a pair of rational-function matrices
\[P\in K^{r\times 2k},\qquad Q\in K^{2k\times r}\]
satisfying the polynomial identity \(A(y)=PQ\). The factorization implies \(\operatorname{rank}_K A(y)\leq2k\), and hence the generic-rank characterization yields \(\nu(M,\Pi)\leq k\). After clearing denominators, the identity can be checked by polynomial arithmetic. Equivalently, vanishing of every \((2k+2)\)-minor of \(A(y)\) certifies the same upper bound, although that encoding may be exponentially large.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A width-\(2k\) factorization of the symbolic parity matrix is an algebraically checkable certificate that no feasible parity family exceeds \(k\) pairs.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Regime Covering Certificates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The factorization is a valid algebraic rank upper witness if the preceding generic-rank theorem holds, but the certificate encoding and verification model need a source. The explanatory derivation should also be removed from the final knowledge statement.

children.title: Min–Max Certificate Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural connection between linear-regime min–max values and covering witnesses.

assumptions_latex: \(A(y)\) is the symbolic skew-symmetric matrix of a represented parity instance over \(K=\mathbb F(y_1,\ldots,y_m)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A nonzero \(2k\)-minor and a width-\(2k\) factorization together certify \(\nu(M,\Pi)=k\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: matching lower and upper generic-rank witnesses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Paired algebraic certificates for the exact optimum in linear matroid parity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A nonzero \(2k\)-minor of \(A(y)\) certifies \(\operatorname{rank}_K A(y)\geq2k\), while an exact factorization
\[A(y)=PQ,\qquad P\in K^{r\times 2k},\qquad Q\in K^{2k\times r}\]
certifies \(\operatorname{rank}_K A(y)\leq2k\). When both witnesses are present, they establish \(\operatorname{rank}_K A(y)=2k\). Through the linear matroid-parity rank correspondence, the same witnesses certify
\[\nu(M,\Pi)=k.\]
Thus lower witnesses from nonvanishing minors and upper witnesses from covering factorizations correspond exactly at the optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero minor gives the lower bound and a matching-width factorization gives the upper bound; together they certify the exact linear-parity optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Min–Max Certificate Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Matching minor and factorization witnesses would certify exact generic rank and hence parity value, but both the rank correspondence and the proposed certificate model require an exact source. The statement also contains proof-style derivation.

assumptions_latex: The matroid is represented by a matrix \(A\in\mathbb F^{r\times 2m}\) whose columns are partitioned into pairs \(P_1,\ldots,P_m\).
Arithmetic in \(\mathbb F\), or in a polynomial-size extension field, is available effectively.

There is a randomized algebraic algorithm that, given \(A\) and its column pairing, returns a feasible set \(J\) of maximum cardinality using a number of field operations polynomial in \(r\) and \(m\). The algorithm may work over a sufficiently large extension of \(\mathbb F\); its failure probability can be made at most \(\varepsilon>0\) with overhead polynomial in \(\log(1/\varepsilon)\).

review_flags: The boundary varies with field, representation model, and current derandomization results.
A claim-specific source is required before fixing a stronger deterministic theorem.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic derandomization boundary, not a universal separation theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Algebraic matroid-parity methods reduce a decision or augmentation step to testing whether a constructed polynomial \(p(\mathbf z)\) is identically zero. Evaluation at a uniformly random point of a sufficiently large finite set gives a polynomial-time test with controllably small error. A deterministic replacement is valid only when one can construct, in polynomial time, a hitting set \(H\) such that every nonzero witness polynomial arising from the instance is nonzero at some \(h\in H\). Thus random evaluation alone does not supply an unconditional deterministic algorithm; deterministic tractability depends on an appropriate hitting set or additional representation structure.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Construct a multigraph \(H\) with vertex set \(V\cup\{r\}\). In the graphic matroid \(M(H)\), the union \(\bigcup_{e\in F}P_e\) is independent if and only if \(F\subseteq E\) is a matching in \(G\). knowledge_statements.title: Integral Polymatroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite integral polymatroids in rank-function form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(f:2^E\to\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) is an integral polymatroid rank function when \(f(\varnothing)=0\), \(f(S)\le f(T)\) for \(S\subseteq T\), and \(f(S)+f(T)\ge f(S\cup T)+f(S\cap T)\) for all \(S,T\subseteq E\). Its polymatroid is \[P(f)=\{x\in\mathbb R_{\ge 0}^E:x(S)\le f(S)\text{ for every }S\subseteq E\}.\] It is called integral because every nonempty face of \(P(f)\) contains an integral point; equivalently, all vertices of \(P(f)\) are integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integral polymatroid is defined by a normalized, nondecreasing, integer-valued submodular rank function through nonnegative subset-sum inequalities.
assumptions_latex: The function \(f:2^E\to\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) is normalized, nondecreasing, and submodular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The polyhedron \(P(f)\) is an integral polymatroid, and its integer points satisfy the displayed subset-sum inequalities.

notation.meaning: The polymatroid polyhedron induced by the rank function.
The coordinate sum over a subset.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V=\biguplus_{e\in E}V_e\), and for \(S\subseteq E\) write \(V_S=\bigcup_{e\in S}V_e\). Define \[r_M(X)=\min_{S\subseteq E}\bigl(|X\setminus V_S|+f(S)\bigr)\qquad(X\subseteq V).\] This is a matroid rank function on \(V\). Moreover, for \(x\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^E\), one has \(x\in P(f)\) if and only if there exists an independent set \(I\) of \(M\) satisfying \(|I\cap V_e|=x_e\) for every \(e\in E\). Thus linear optimization over integral polymatroid points reduces to weighted matroid independence after copying each element weight across its fiber.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expanding each polymatroid element into a finite fiber produces a matroid whose independent-set projections are precisely the integral polymatroid points.

knowledge_statements.title: Reduction Validity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits of exact finite-fiber reduction outside finite integral polymatroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite-fiber projection \(\pi(I)_e=|I\cap V_e|\) always has integral coordinates, so the expansion theorem represents the integer points of an integral polymatroid, not every point of its continuous polyhedron. Integer-valued singleton ranks are also needed to choose fibers with \(|V_e|=f(\{e\})\). For example, if \(E=\{e\}\), \(f(\varnothing)=0\), and \(f(\{e\})=\tfrac12\), then \[P(f)=[0,\tfrac12].\] Its fractional vertex \(\tfrac12\) cannot be a fiber-cardinality projection, and linear optimization over the projected independent sets cannot reproduce the optimum of every objective over \(P(f)\). Moreover, without normalization, monotonicity, and submodularity, the proposed rank formula need not satisfy the matroid rank axioms. Thus the stated finite-fiber reduction is valid for finite integral polymatroids and does not extend unchanged to arbitrary fractional or nonsubmodular set functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fiber projections describe integer polymatroid points; fractional vertices and violations of the polymatroid axioms fall outside this exact reduction.
assumptions_latex: A proposed reduction uses finite fibers whose cardinalities encode coordinate capacities.
The reduction is required to preserve the relevant feasible integer points and linear-optimization values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The standard finite-fiber reduction requires finite integer-valued polymatroid data and does not exactly preserve fractional vertices or arbitrary non-polymatroid systems.

children.title: Polymatroid Greedy Optimization
children.top_down_role: Greedy optimization over polymatroid feasible regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Polymatroid Greedy Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Edmonds greedy rule for finite polymatroids and nonnegative weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(S_0=\varnothing\) and \(S_i=\{e_1,\ldots,e_i\}\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n\). Define the greedy vector by \[x_{e_i}=f(S_i)-f(S_{i-1})\qquad(i=1,\ldots,n).\] Then \(x\in B(f)\subseteq P(f)\), and \(c^Tx\ge c^Ty\) for every \(y\in P(f)\). The algorithm therefore sorts the weights, evaluates \(f\) on the resulting prefix chain, outputs these successive increments, and stops after \(n\) rank evaluations. Ties may be ordered arbitrarily; every resulting vector is optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sort nonnegative weights and assign successive rank increments along the prefix chain; the resulting base maximizes the linear objective.
assumptions_latex: The function \(f:2^E\to\mathbb R\) is normalized, nondecreasing, and submodular.
The elements are ordered so that \(c_{e_1}\ge\cdots\ge c_{e_n}\ge 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The greedy increment vector maximizes \(c^Tx\) over \(P(f)\), and hence also over \(B(f)\).

notation.meaning: The prefix consisting of the first ordered elements.

knowledge_statements.title: Total-Dual-Integrality Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Chain-supported integral dual certificate for nonnegative integral objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the primal program \(\max\{c^Tx:x(S)\le f(S)\ (S\subseteq E),\ x\ge 0\}\), assign dual multipliers \(y_{S_i}=c_{e_i}-c_{e_{i+1}}\) to the prefix inequalities and zero to all other subset inequalities. These multipliers are nonnegative integers and satisfy \(\sum_{S\ni e}y_S\ge c_e\) for every \(e\in E\). Their objective value is \[\sum_{i=1}^n(c_{e_i}-c_{e_{i+1}})f(S_i),\] which equals the value of the greedy primal vector. Feasibility, integrality, and equality of the two displayed values certify optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integral differences between consecutive sorted weights give a chain-supported dual certificate whose value equals the greedy solution's value.
assumptions_latex: The function \(f:2^E\to\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) is normalized, nondecreasing, and submodular.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The integral chain multipliers form a checkable dual certificate matching the greedy primal value.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Order \(E\) so that \(c_{e_1}\ge\cdots\ge c_{e_n}\ge0\), put \(S_i=\{e_1,\ldots,e_i\}\), and set \(c_{e_{n+1}}=0\). The greedy primal solution and chain dual solution are \[x^*_{e_i}=f(S_i)-f(S_{i-1}),\qquad y^*_{S_i}=c_{e_i}-c_{e_{i+1}}.\] All other dual multipliers are zero. They are feasible and satisfy \[c^Tx^*=\sum_{i=1}^n(c_{e_i}-c_{e_{i+1}})f(S_i).\] When \(f\) and \(c\) are integral, both solutions are integral. Thus greedy optimization constructs the integral dual optimum required by total dual integrality for these objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The greedy increments and consecutive weight differences form primal and integral dual optima with equal value, explaining the polymatroid TDI correspondence.
knowledge_statements.title: Greedy–TDI Correspondence

children.title: Integrality Failure Boundaries

knowledge_statements.title: Integrality Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp singleton obstruction to primal integrality when rank integrality is removed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E=\{e\}\), \(f(\varnothing)=0\), and \(f(\{e\})=\tfrac12\). This function is normalized, nondecreasing, and submodular, but not integer-valued. Its polymatroid is \[P(f)=\{x_e\in\mathbb R_{\ge 0}:x_e\le\tfrac12\}=[0,\tfrac12],\] whose nonzero vertex is fractional. For the integral objective \(c_e=1\), the greedy optimum is \(x_e^*=\tfrac12\) with value \(\tfrac12\), so no integral primal point attains the linear-programming optimum. Hence submodularity alone does not imply polyhedral integrality; integer-valued rank data is essential for the integral-vertex and integral-greedy conclusions. This example does not by itself refute total dual integrality, which is a property of the constraint system's dual certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A singleton rank of one half yields a fractional optimal vertex, showing that submodularity without integer-valued rank data does not ensure primal polyhedral integrality.
assumptions_latex: The rank bound may be nonintegral while remaining normalized, nondecreasing, and submodular.
Integrality of polymatroid vertices and greedy primal optima is desired.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without integer-valued rank data, polymatroid vertices and greedy primal optima may be fractional; this alone does not establish failure of total dual integrality.

children.title: Polymatroid Intersection
children.top_down_role: Structural aspects of common feasible regions for polymatroids.

knowledge_statements.title: Polymatroid Intersection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cardinality form of the integral polymatroid-intersection theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E\) be finite and let \(f_1,f_2:2^E\to\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) be normalized, nondecreasing, submodular functions. For \(i\in\{1,2\}\), define \(P(f_i)=\{x\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^E:x(S)\le f_i(S)\text{ for every }S\subseteq E\}\). Then \(P(f_1)\cap P(f_2)\) is an integral polytope and
\[\max\{x(E):x\in P(f_1)\cap P(f_2)\}=\min_{S\subseteq E}\bigl(f_1(S)+f_2(E\setminus S)\bigr).\]
Consequently, the maximum is attained by an integral vector whenever the intersection is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum total size of a common polymatroid vector equals a submodular cut minimum, and integer rank functions guarantee an integer optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) are normalized, integer-valued, nondecreasing, and submodular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P(f_1)\cap P(f_2)\) is integral and satisfies the displayed min–max equality.

notation.meaning: The sum of coordinates of x indexed by S.
The polymatroid determined by rank function f_i.

review_flags: Exact polymatroid-intersection theorem locator is absent from the supplied inventory.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem is standard, precise, and appropriately classified, but no inspectable source supports its integrality and min–max claims.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Common-Independent-Set Polytope of Two Matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank-inequality description of the convex hull of sets independent in both matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let (E,\mathcal M_1) and (E,\mathcal M_2) be matroids with rank functions r_1 and r_2. Then
\[
\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^I:I\in\mathcal M_1\cap\mathcal M_2\}
=
\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}_+^E:\sum_{e\in A}x_e\le\min\{r_1(A),r_2(A)\}\text{ for every }A\subseteq E\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex hull of incidence vectors of sets independent in both of two matroids consists exactly of the nonnegative vectors satisfying every subset-rank inequality for both matroids, equivalently the bound by the minimum of their two ranks.
assumptions_latex: (E,\mathcal M_1)\text{ and }(E,\mathcal M_2)\text{ are matroids on the same finite ground set}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{conv}\{\chi^I:I\in\mathcal M_1\cap\mathcal M_2\}=\{x\in\mathbb{R}_+^E:x(A)\le\min(r_1(A),r_2(A))\ \forall A\subseteq E\}

children.title: Integer Decomposition Property
children.top_down_role: Decomposition behavior of integral points in scaled polyhedra.

knowledge_statements.title: Integer Decomposition Property
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer decomposition for an integral polymatroid polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E\) be finite, let \(f:2^E\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) be normalized, nondecreasing, and submodular, and let \(P(f)=\{x\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^E:x(S)\le f(S)\text{ for every }S\subseteq E\}\). For every integer \(k\ge1\) and every \(z\in kP(f)\cap\mathbb Z^E\), there exist \(z^{(1)},\ldots,z^{(k)}\in P(f)\cap\mathbb Z^E\) such that
\[z=z^{(1)}+\cdots+z^{(k)}.\]
Thus every lattice point in an integral dilation decomposes into lattice points of the original polymatroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every lattice point in a positive integer dilation of an integral polymatroid is a sum of lattice points from that polymatroid.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is normalized, integer-valued, nondecreasing, and submodular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(kP(f)\cap\mathbb Z^E=(P(f)\cap\mathbb Z^E)+\cdots+(P(f)\cap\mathbb Z^E)\), with \(k\) summands.

notation.meaning: The scalar dilation of P(f) by k.

children.title: Intersection–Decomposition Interface
children.top_down_role: Links between intersection structure and integer decomposability.

knowledge_statements.title: Intersection–Decomposition Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer decomposition within the intersection of two integral polymatroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f_1,f_2:2^E\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) be normalized, nondecreasing, submodular functions on a finite set \(E\), and put \(Q=P(f_1)\cap P(f_2)\). For every integer \(k\ge1\) and every \(z\in kQ\cap\mathbb Z^E\), there are integral common polymatroid vectors \(z^{(1)},\ldots,z^{(k)}\in Q\cap\mathbb Z^E\) satisfying
\[z=z^{(1)}+\cdots+z^{(k)}.\]
Hence the polymatroid-intersection integrality mechanism is stable under integer dilation and yields the integer decomposition property for \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integer point in a dilation of two intersecting integral polymatroids decomposes into integer points feasible for both polymatroids.
assumptions_latex: \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) are normalized, integer-valued, nondecreasing, and submodular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(kQ\cap\mathbb Z^E=(Q\cap\mathbb Z^E)+\cdots+(Q\cap\mathbb Z^E)\), with \(k\) summands.

notation.meaning: The intersection of the two polymatroid polytopes.
The scalar dilation of Q by k.

review_flags: A source explicitly establishing integer decomposition for polymatroid intersections is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claimed integer-decomposition theorem for a two-polymatroid intersection requires an explicit authoritative locator; ordinary intersection integrality alone would not suffice as evidence.

children.title: Decomposition Failure Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition Failure Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Three polymatroids already destroy the two-polymatroid integrality mechanism.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E=\{000,011,101,110\}\). For each coordinate \(j\in\{1,2,3\}\), let \(M_j\) be the partition matroid imposing capacity one on each class of triples having a fixed value in coordinate \(j\). The vector \(x\in\mathbb R^E\) with \(x_e=\tfrac12\) for every \(e\in E\) belongs to \(P(M_1)\cap P(M_2)\cap P(M_3)\) and has \(x(E)=2\). Any two distinct triples in \(E\) agree in some coordinate, so every common independent set has size at most one. Thus the three-polymatroid intersection is nonintegral, and the two-polymatroid decomposition conclusion cannot be extended without additional structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A four-triple three-dimensional matching instance has fractional value two but integral value one, showing failure for intersections of three matroids.
assumptions_latex: Each \(P(M_j)\) is the independent-set polytope of the stated partition matroid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P(M_1)\cap P(M_2)\cap P(M_3)\) is not integral.

notation.meaning: The independent-set polytope of partition matroid M_j.
The coordinate associated with triple e.

children.title: Generalized Polymatroid Structure
children.top_down_role: Feasible-region structure specific to generalized polymatroids.

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Polymatroid Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized polymatroid defined by an integral paramodular pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E\) be finite. A pair \((p,b)\) with \(p,b:2^E\to\mathbb R\), \(p(\varnothing)=b(\varnothing)=0\), is paramodular when \(p\) is supermodular, \(b\) is submodular, and
\[b(X)-p(Y)\ge b(X\setminus Y)-p(Y\setminus X)\qquad(X,Y\subseteq E).\]
Its generalized polymatroid is
\[Q(p,b)=\{x\in\mathbb R^E:p(S)\le x(S)\le b(S)\text{ for every }S\subseteq E\}.\]
It is integral when \(p\) and \(b\) are integer-valued; in that case every nonempty face contains an integral point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generalized polymatroid is the set of vectors bounded below and above on every subset by a paramodular supermodular–submodular pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q(p,b)=\{x:p(S)\le x(S)\le b(S)\text{ for all }S\subseteq E\}\).

notation.meaning: The sum of coordinates of x over S.
The generalized polymatroid defined by p and b.

review_flags: No generalized-polymatroid definition locator was supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The paramodular-pair definition is plausible, but neither it nor the appended integrality assertion has an inspectable source. The latter is a property rather than part of the definition and particularly requires support.

children.title: Submodular-Flow Feasible Regions
children.top_down_role: Feasibility structures arising in submodular-flow formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Submodular-Flow Feasible Regions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible submodular flows with box-constrained arcs and base-polyhedron boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite digraph, let \(f:2^V\to\mathbb R\) be submodular with \(f(\varnothing)=f(V)=0\), and let \(\ell,u\in(\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty,+\infty\})^A\) satisfy \(\ell\le u\). For \(x\in\mathbb R^A\), define \(\partial x(v)=x(\delta^-(v))-x(\delta^+(v))\). The submodular-flow feasible region is
\[F(D,f,\ell,u)=\{x\in\mathbb R^A:\ell\le x\le u,\ \partial x\in B(f)\},\]
where \(B(f)=\{y\in\mathbb R^V:y(S)\le f(S)\text{ for all }S\subseteq V,\ y(V)=0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A submodular flow obeys arc bounds and has its net boundary vector in a submodular base polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(D,f,\ell,u)=\{x:\ell\le x\le u,\ \partial x\in B(f)\}\).
review_flags: Supplied network-flow locators do not cover the submodular base constraint.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is coherent and fits the leaf, but the inventory locators cover ordinary flows rather than the base-polyhedron constraint defining submodular flows.

children.title: Generalized-Polymatroid Flow Reductions
children.top_down_role: Structural reductions connecting generalized polymatroids to submodular flows.

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized-Polymatroid Flow Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-extra-vertex representation of a generalized polymatroid by submodular-flow boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a paramodular pair \((p,b)\) on \(E\), introduce \(s\notin E\) and define \(f:2^{E\cup\{s\}}\to\mathbb R\) by
\[f(X)=b(X),\qquad f(X\cup\{s\})=-p(E\setminus X)\qquad(X\subseteq E).\]
Then \(f\) is submodular and
\[Q(p,b)=\{x|_E:x\in B(f)\}.\]
Equivalently, on the star with arcs \(s\to e\) for \(e\in E\), an arc vector \(z\) satisfies \(\partial z|_E=z\) and \(\partial z(s)=-z(E)\); hence \(z\in Q(p,b)\) exactly when \(\partial z\in B(f)\). Linear objectives are preserved coordinatewise by this reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding one root converts generalized-polymatroid lower and upper bounds into a base-polyhedron boundary constraint on a directed star.
assumptions_latex: \((p,b)\) is a paramodular pair on finite \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q(p,b)=\{x|_E:x\in B(f)\}=\{z\in\mathbb R^E:\partial z\in B(f)\}\) under the star identification.

notation.meaning: The additional root element or star vertex.
The lifted submodular function on the extended ground set.

review_flags: The exact lifted-base representation requires a generalized-polymatroid source locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The lifted-base and directed-star representation is nontrivial and needs a specific generalized-polymatroid or submodular-flow source locator.

children.title: Flow-Interface Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where the generalized-polymatroid flow correspondence breaks down.

knowledge_statements.title: Flow-Interface Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The crossing inequality is necessary for the lifted function to be submodular.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E=\{1,2\}\), define \(b(\varnothing)=0\), \(b(\{1\})=0\), \(b(\{2\})=1\), \(b(E)=1\), and define \(p(\varnothing)=p(\{1\})=p(\{2\})=0\), \(p(E)=1\). Although \(b\) is submodular and \(p\) is supermodular, the crossing inequality fails for \(X=\{1\}\) and \(Y=E\), since
\[b(X)-p(Y)=-1<0=b(X\setminus Y)-p(Y\setminus X).\]
For the one-root lift, \(f(\{1\})=0\), \(f(\{s\})=-1\), \(f(\{1,s\})=0\), and \(f(\varnothing)=0\). Consequently,
\[f(\{1\})+f(\{s\})=-1<0=f(\{1,s\})+f(\varnothing),\]
so \(f\) is not submodular. Thus the star construction is not a submodular-flow reduction without paramodularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separate submodularity and supermodularity do not suffice: violating the crossing inequality makes the lifted boundary function non-submodular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The lifted \(f\) is not submodular, so the generalized-polymatroid flow interface fails.

notation.meaning: The added root element in the lifted construction.
The function obtained from p and b by the one-root lift.

review_flags: The corrected, directly checkable boundary example lacks a supplied scholarly locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Continuation Property Is Equivalent to Union Closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization of union-closed accessible set systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(E,\mathcal F)$ be an accessible set system. The following are equivalent: (a) for every $X\subseteq Y\subset E$ and $z\in E\setminus Y$, if $X\cup\{z\}\in\mathcal F$ and $Y\in\mathcal F$, then $Y\cup\{z\}\in\mathcal F$; (b) $\mathcal F$ is closed under union.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an accessible set system, the continuation property is equivalent to closure of the feasible family under union.
assumptions_latex: (E,\mathcal F)\text{ is an accessible set system}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left[\forall X\subseteq Y\subset E\ \forall z\in E\setminus Y:\ (X\cup\{z\}\in\mathcal F\land Y\in\mathcal F)\Rightarrow Y\cup\{z\}\in\mathcal F\right]\iff\left[\mathcal F\text{ is closed under union}\right]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Greedoid
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Axiomatic definition of a greedoid feasible-set system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set system $(E,\mathcal F)$ is a greedoid if $\varnothing\in\mathcal F$ and, for all $X,Y\in\mathcal F$ with $|X|<|Y|$, there exists $y\in Y\setminus X$ such that $X\cup\{y\}\in\mathcal F$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A greedoid is a set system satisfying the empty-set axiom and the augmentation axiom: whenever two feasible sets have different sizes, an element of the larger can be added to the smaller while preserving feasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (E,\mathcal F)\text{ is a greedoid}\iff \varnothing\in\mathcal F\ \land\ \forall X,Y\in\mathcal F,\ |X|<|Y|\Rightarrow\exists y\in Y\setminus X:\ X\cup\{y\}\in\mathcal F

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Accessibility and the Anti-Exchange Property
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes accessibility of a union-closed set system through its associated closure operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(E,\mathcal F)$ be a set system such that $\varnothing\in\mathcal F$ and $\mathcal F$ is closed under union, and let $\tau$ be the closure operator of Proposition 14.4. Then $(E,\mathcal F)$ is accessible if and only if, for every $X\subseteq E$ and distinct $y,z\in E\setminus\tau(X)$, $$z\in\tau(X\cup\{y\})\implies y\notin\tau(X\cup\{z\}).$$
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A union-closed set system containing the empty set is accessible exactly when its associated closure operator has the anti-exchange property.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (E,\mathcal F)\text{ is accessible}\iff \forall X\subseteq E\ \forall y\ne z\in E\setminus\tau(X),\ z\in\tau(X\cup\{y\})\Rightarrow y\notin\tau(X\cup\{z\}).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Greedy Extension Algorithm for a Greedoid
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Repeatedly selects an objective-maximizing feasible one-element extension without asserting global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a greedoid $(E,\mathcal F)$ and oracle access that decides whether $X\in\mathcal F$ and returns $c(X)$ for $c:2^E\to\mathbb R$, initialize $F:=\varnothing$. While there exists $e\in E\setminus F$ with $F\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal F$, choose such an $e$ maximizing $c(F\cup\{e\})$ and set $F:=F\cup\{e\}$. If no such element exists, stop and return $F$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Begin with the empty set and repeatedly add a feasible element whose resulting set has maximum objective value among all feasible one-element extensions. Stop when no feasible extension exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\in\mathcal F\quad\text{and, at termination,}\quad \nexists e\in E\setminus F\text{ such that }F\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal F.

children.title: Accessibility Axiom
children.top_down_role: The accessibility component of greedoid feasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Accessibility Axiom
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deletion accessibility for a finite greedoid feasible-set system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E\) be finite and let \(\mathcal F\subseteq2^E\) with \(\varnothing\in\mathcal F\). The accessibility axiom is
\[X\in\mathcal F,\ X\ne\varnothing\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{there exists }e\in X\text{ such that }X\setminus\{e\}\in\mathcal F.\]
Thus every nonempty feasible set admits at least one feasible one-element deletion. Together with the greedoid augmentation axiom, accessibility makes \((E,\mathcal F)\) a greedoid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty feasible set must contain an element whose deletion leaves another feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall X\in\mathcal F\setminus\{\varnothing\}\ \exists e\in X:\ X\setminus\{e\}\in\mathcal F\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The accessibility condition is standard, explicit, and correctly classified, but no greedoid source locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set system is accessible if the empty set is feasible and every nonempty feasible set admits deletion of some element while remaining feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (E,\mathcal F)\text{ is accessible}\iff \varnothing\in\mathcal F\ \land\ \forall X\in\mathcal F\setminus\{\varnothing\}\ \exists x\in X:\ X\setminus\{x\}\in\mathcal F

children.title: Feasible Continuation Sets
children.top_down_role: Continuation choices available from feasible sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasible Continuation Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elements that extend a feasible greedoid set by one step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((E,\mathcal F)\) be a greedoid and let \(X\in\mathcal F\). The feasible continuation set of \(X\) is
\[\Gamma(X)=\{e\in E\setminus X:X\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal F\}.\]
The greedoid augmentation axiom is equivalently expressed as follows: whenever \(X,Y\in\mathcal F\) and \(|X|<|Y|\), one has
\[\Gamma(X)\cap(Y\setminus X)\ne\varnothing.\]
Hence a larger feasible set always supplies at least one feasible next element for the smaller set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The continuation set contains precisely the unused elements that can be appended while preserving feasibility; augmentation guarantees a continuation from any larger feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Gamma(X)=\{e\in E\setminus X:X\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal F\}\).

notation.meaning: The feasible continuation set at X.

review_flags: No greedoid continuation-set source locator was supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The continuation-set definition and augmentation reformulation are precise, but both lack a specific greedoid source locator.

children.title: Prefix Feasibility
children.top_down_role: Feasibility organization along prefixes of admissible constructions.

knowledge_statements.title: Prefix Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accessibility is equivalent to existence of a feasible ordering for every feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E\) be finite and let \(\mathcal F\subseteq2^E\) contain \(\varnothing\). The system satisfies accessibility if and only if every \(X\in\mathcal F\) has an ordering \(X=\{e_1,\ldots,e_k\}\) such that
\[\{e_1,\ldots,e_i\}\in\mathcal F\qquad(0\le i\le k),\]
where the prefix for \(i=0\) is \(\varnothing\). Such an ordering is called a feasible ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite feasible system is accessible exactly when every feasible set can be ordered so that all initial prefixes remain feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Accessibility holds if and only if every \(X\in\mathcal F\) admits a feasible ordering.

notation.meaning: An ordering of the elements of a feasible set X.

review_flags: No source locator for the accessibility–prefix equivalence was supplied.

children.title: Continuation Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Obstructions to extending feasible sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Continuation Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accessibility alone does not imply greedoid augmentation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E=\{a,b,c\}\) and
\[\mathcal F=\{\varnothing,\{a\},\{b\},\{a,c\}\}.\]
This feasible system is accessible: each singleton deletes to \(\varnothing\), and \(\{a,c\}\) deletes \(c\) to obtain \(\{a\}\). However, for \(X=\{b\}\) and \(Y=\{a,c\}\), one has \(|X|<|Y|\) but
\[\Gamma(X)\cap(Y\setminus X)=\varnothing,\]
because neither \(\{a,b\}\) nor \(\{b,c\}\) is feasible. Thus accessibility and prefix feasibility do not by themselves guarantee the continuation property or define a greedoid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An accessible four-set system has a smaller feasible set that cannot be extended by either element of a larger feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The system is accessible but violates greedoid augmentation.

notation.meaning: The feasible continuation set of X.
The smaller and larger feasible sets in the counterexample.

children.title: Antimatroid Structures
children.top_down_role: Feasible-set organization specific to antimatroids.

assumptions_latex: The family \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^E\) has ground support \(E=\bigcup_{F\in\mathcal F}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair \((E,\mathcal F)\) is an antimatroid exactly when it satisfies accessibility and union closure.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard finite feasible-set definition of an antimatroid
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite, loopless feasible-set formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A pair \((E,\mathcal F)\) is an antimatroid if \(\varnothing\in\mathcal F\) and the following hold. Accessibility: for every nonempty \(F\in\mathcal F\), there exists \(x\in F\) such that \(F\setminus\{x\}\in\mathcal F\). Union closure: for all \(F_1,F_2\in\mathcal F\), one has \(F_1\cup F_2\in\mathcal F\). Because \(E\) is finite and equals the union of all feasible sets, union closure also gives \(E\in\mathcal F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An antimatroid is a finite accessible set system whose feasible sets are closed under union and collectively cover the ground set.
knowledge_statements.title: Antimatroid Structures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite loopless feasible-set definition is mathematically standard and fits the Antimatroid Structures container, but no inspectable citation or specific locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An antimatroid is an accessible set system satisfying the equivalent continuation and union-closure conditions, hence one whose feasible family is closed under union.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (E,\mathcal F)\text{ is an antimatroid}\iff \mathcal F\text{ is closed under union}

children.title: Convex Geometry Structures
children.top_down_role: Closure-system organization specific to convex geometries.

assumptions_latex: The map \(\operatorname{cl}:2^E\to2^E\) is a closure operator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair \((E,\operatorname{cl})\) is a convex geometry exactly when empty-set closure and anti-exchange hold.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard finite closure-operator definition of a convex geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite anti-exchange closure formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A closure operator \(\operatorname{cl}\) is extensive, isotone, and idempotent. The pair \((E,\operatorname{cl})\) is a convex geometry if \(\operatorname{cl}(\varnothing)=\varnothing\) and it satisfies anti-exchange: for every closed set \(C=\operatorname{cl}(C)\) and distinct \(x,y\in E\setminus C\),
\[y\in\operatorname{cl}(C\cup\{x\})\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x\notin\operatorname{cl}(C\cup\{y\}).\]
Equivalently, its closed sets form an intersection-closed family containing \(\varnothing\) and \(E\), with closure obtained by intersecting all closed supersets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite convex geometry is a closure system with empty-set closure and the anti-exchange property for two distinct points outside a closed set.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Geometry Structures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The anti-exchange definition fits the Convex Geometry Structures container, but it has no citation. The final equivalence sentence should also be checked against a source because intersection closure with empty and full sets alone does not characterize convex geometries without the anti-exchange condition.

children.title: Closure–Feasibility Duality
children.top_down_role: Dual viewpoints relating closure structure to feasible-set structure.

assumptions_latex: The pair \((E,\mathcal F)\) is a finite antimatroid.
The family of complementary sets is \(\mathcal C=\{E\setminus F:F\in\mathcal F\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility and closedness are complementary: \(F\in\mathcal F\iff E\setminus F\in\mathcal C\).

notation.meaning: closure induced by the closed sets

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard complement duality between finite antimatroids and convex geometries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complement duality on a fixed finite ground set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(\mathcal C=\{E\setminus F:F\in\mathcal F\}\). Union closure of \(\mathcal F\) makes \(\mathcal C\) intersection closed, and its closure operator is
\[\operatorname{cl}(X)=\bigcap\{C\in\mathcal C:X\subseteq C\}.\]
The resulting \((E,\operatorname{cl})\) is a convex geometry, and
\[F\in\mathcal F\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad E\setminus F\text{ is closed}.\]
Conversely, complements of the closed sets of any finite convex geometry form the feasible sets of an antimatroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complementation converts feasible antimatroid sets into closed convex-geometry sets, with closure given by intersection of closed supersets; the construction also works in reverse.
knowledge_statements.title: Closure–Feasibility Duality

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complement construction has the correct duality role and is standard for finite antimatroids and convex geometries, but no source or inspectable locator supports the asserted converse and induced closure structure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure Operator Induced by Union-Closed Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction of a closure operator from complements of a union-closed feasible family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(E,\mathcal F)$ be a set system such that $\varnothing\in\mathcal F$ and $\mathcal F$ is closed under union. For $A\subseteq E$, define $\tau(A):=\bigcap\{X\subseteq E:A\subseteq X,\ E\setminus X\in\mathcal F\}$. Then $\tau$ is a closure operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a union-closed feasible family containing the empty set, intersecting all supersets of a set whose complements are feasible defines a closure operator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \tau\text{ is a closure operator}

source_refs.locator: Generalizations of Matroids / 14.1. Greedoids / Proposition 14.4

knowledge_statements.title: Closure Operator Induced by Union-Closed Feasibility

children.title: Antimatroid–Convex-Geometry Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Translation between antimatroid and convex-geometry presentations.

assumptions_latex: All structures use the same finite ground set \(E\).
Antimatroids are loopless, and convex geometries satisfy \(\operatorname{cl}(\varnothing)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Complementation induces mutually inverse correspondences between antimatroids and convex geometries on \(E\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bijection between finite structures, not merely an analogy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The assignments
\[\mathcal F\longmapsto\mathcal C_{\mathcal F}:=\{E\setminus F:F\in\mathcal F\}\]
and
\[\mathcal C\longmapsto\mathcal F_{\mathcal C}:=\{E\setminus C:C\in\mathcal C\}\]
are mutually inverse. Under these assignments, accessibility and union closure of \(\mathcal F\) correspond to anti-exchange and intersection closure of \(\mathcal C\), respectively. Hence antimatroid feasible-set systems on \(E\) are in bijection with convex geometries on \(E\), and applying the correspondence twice returns the original family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Taking complements gives a reversible, one-to-one correspondence between finite antimatroids and finite convex geometries on the same ground set.
knowledge_statements.title: Antimatroid–Convex-Geometry Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A theorem-level bijective correspondence fits this terminal container, but it lacks evidence. The componentwise claim that accessibility and union closure correspond respectively to anti-exchange and intersection closure requires source confirmation and careful formulation.

children.title: Branching Greedoids
children.top_down_role: Greedoid structures arising from rooted branching systems.

assumptions_latex: The directed graph \(D=(V,A)\\) is finite and has a distinguished root \(r\in V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible arborescence edge sets form the branching greedoid \((A,\mathcal F_r)\).

notation.meaning: directed graph with arc set as ground set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed, arc-ground-set version rooted at one vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F_r\) consist of those \(X\subseteq A\) for which the subgraph formed by \(X\), its incident vertices, and \(r\) is an out-arborescence rooted at \(r\): every represented vertex is reachable from \(r\), every represented vertex other than \(r\) has indegree one in \(X\), and the underlying undirected graph is acyclic. Then \((A,\mathcal F_r)\) is called the branching greedoid of \((D,r)\). Its feasible sets are precisely the arc sets of partial rooted out-arborescences.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed branching greedoid has as feasible sets the arc sets of partial out-arborescences rooted at a fixed vertex.
knowledge_statements.title: Branching Greedoids

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits Branching Greedoids and clearly selects the directed arc-ground-set convention, but branching-greedoid conventions vary and no authoritative definition with a section or page locator is cited.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directed and Undirected Branching Greedoids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Names the greedoids constructed from rooted directed arborescences and rooted undirected trees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graph $G$ with root $r$, the greedoid whose feasible sets are the edge sets of arborescences rooted at $r$ in the directed case, or trees containing $r$ in the undirected case, is called the directed branching greedoid or undirected branching greedoid of $G$, respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The greedoid formed by rooted arborescences is called a directed branching greedoid, and the corresponding greedoid formed by root-containing undirected trees is called an undirected branching greedoid.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal F\text{ is the applicable rooted branching edge-set family}
(E(G),\mathcal F)\text{ is the greedoid established in Proposition 14.6}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (E(G),\mathcal F)\text{ is called the directed or undirected branching greedoid of }G.

In the directed case, let $\mathcal F$ be the family of edge sets of arborescences in $G$ rooted at $r$; in the undirected case, let $\mathcal F$ be the family of edge sets of trees in $G$ containing $r$.
